1.	How many men, not claiming to be conscientious objectors, have refused, to date, to report for training under the National Resources Mobilization Act?

3.	What action has the government taken, or proposes to take, in regard to men, not claiming to be conscientious objectors, who refuse to report for training?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
I think I should answer parts 1 and 3 orally at the moment, and then I would ask the hon. member to permit this to be made an order for return, now tabled, in order that the answers may be fully explained in connection with the other two questions.
As to the first question, the number of men unaccounted for is 169. I should explain that this is not necessarily a case of refusing to report, because in many instances the notices did not reach the men.
The third question asks what action the government has taken, or proposes to take, in regard to men, not claiming to be conscientious objectors, who refuse to report for training. The answer is that all cases have been or will be referred to the police for necessary action. Reports to date indicate that an appreciable number of men notified to report at training centres had enlisted in the armed forces or were students taking their training at universities. Others had

Questions as Orders for Returns

maintopic: CHRISTMAS LEAVE TO MILITARY AND AIR FORCES AND GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an
order for return, now tabled. But if the house would permit I should like to add a verbal statement with respect to this general question, either now or later. Possibly I could do it now.
On November 11 last my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), issued a statement to the press in regard to the proposed Christmas and New Year's leave arrangements for members of the Canadian Army on active service in Canada. In the house on November 28, and in reply to the question from the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart), I again gave information in regard to the arrangements for leave for the army, and also at that time pointed out the impossibility of making any special holiday leave arrangements for the Royal Canadian Air Force. I would like, at this time, to amplify these statements.
In the first place, may I say that the guiding factor in the consideration of leave privileges to men on active service must be the defence and safety of the country and the obligations we are under by way of our war commitments. Under routine orders for the Canadian active service force, the members of the Canadian Army may be granted leave not exceeding fourteen days with pay upon completion of six months' continuous service with the Canadian active service force, and a further fourteen days' leave upon the completion of each subsequent period of twelve months. The six days' leave at Christmas or the New Year, which has already been announced, is in addition to these regular periods, and while it is hoped that the maximum number possible can avail themselves of the privilege, it is limited to the conditions that not more than fifty per cent of the unit may be absent at one time, and, furthermore, that the commanding officer must take into consideration the nature of the service being undertaken by the man concerned, and the necessity of having certain types of training completed speedily.
I realize that in cases where men are far distant from their homes a total absence of six days from their unit will not permit them to spend any time with their families. In such cases special arrangements are authorized in that where a man has not used up his regular fourteen days' leave, there may, with the permission of his commanding officer, be added to his six days' leave such number of days as he has available in order to enable him to carry out a lengthy journey.
In so far as the Royal Canadian Air Force is concerned, however, the situation is not by any means parallel. The entire personnel of the force is engaged either upon important

Questions as Orders jor Returns
defensive operations or on the intensive programme of training flying personnel so urgently required for service overseas.
Under normal conditions personnel engaged in active and continuous flying are granted, as far as possible, twelve days' leave every three months, and fourteen days' leave every six months is granted to non-flying personnel. It will be readily realized, however, by hon. members that at no one time can any substantial percentage of the operational defence force be spared from their immediate duties.
The joint air training plan is engaged upon a programme of extreme importance and urgency. The courses are intensive, and continuous, and any interruption occasioned by the release for a period either of the pupils or the instructional and administrative personnel causes serious delay in the output of trained pilots, observers, air gunners, and wireless operators. I cannot feel that under the present circumstances any special grant of holiday leave can be justified. Under present arrangements pupils in the flying schools are treated as liberally as possible in* the provision of forty-eight-hour passes when their commanding officers feel that this can be done without interruption of their training. At the conclusion of their course it is the practice of the force to grant adequate leave to enable them to visit their families before embarking for an active theatre of war or proceeding on other duties. Beyond this I do not feel I can at present go.
Before leaving this question I would make emphatic reference again to the practice common to all the defence services of endeavouring to ensure an adequate period of embarkation leave for all members of the forces before they leave their training stations either for defensive positions in Canada or for overseas. In all cases where units are now garrisoning vulnerable areas or are en route overseas, opportunity has already been afforded to the personnel to see their homes and families before leaving.
Many representations have been made both in the public press and directly to my colleagues and myself on the question of the provision of free transportation for members of the forces proceeding on leave. I feel that many of those who make these representations do not realize the magnitude of the question.
I have made careful inquiry into the practice during the last war and I find that in Canada free transportation was never provided for troops proceeding on ordinary leave. In certain cases men returning invalided from overseas, when their condition permitted it, were given free transportation to proceed on leave to their homes, and
return transportation to the hospital where their medical treatment was to be continued. In 1915-16, when the gathering of the harvest was considered to be a work of national importance, free transportation to a maximum distance of 300 miles was provided for those proceeding on harvest leave.
In the present war the scale of pay and dependents' allowance is considerably in excess of that paid during the war of 1914-18. Members of the forces proceeding on ordinary leave are entitled to return tickets at single fare rates. My colleagues and I are agreed that any further financial concessions cannot be made under the present circumstances.
I do not wish hon. members to think that I am not without the greatest sympathy for families who are widely separated on account of the fact that their sons and husbands are on active service, particularly at the Christmas and New Year festival, but I must remind them that at the present time we must all, perforce, subordinate our natural desires and inclinations to the exigencies of war service.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before this motion is put I should like to suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to you, as Speaker, that some consideration be given to the members of the sessional staff of the house. During the past fifteen or sixteen months the house has met infrequently, and to my mind we are in danger of losing the services of some of the experienced help we now have. We may have to content ourselves with inexperienced help in the future unless something is done. I do not know what the government has in mind, but from conversations which I have had with hon. members on all sides I know there is a feeling that some consideration should be given at this time to the sessional staff. I hold the view that the government ought to be something in the nature of a model employer. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
The internal economy commission met to consider the question of the payment of the sessional staff between this part of the session and the next part after we meet in February. It has been found that the payment of the sessional staff during the two months' adjournment, over December and January, would involve the expenditure of SI,276.83 per day, or a total of $79,163.46.
There are 260 sessional clerks and employees. For example, there are 130 stenographers who receive $5 per day, which totals $650 per

day. It will be realized that the rate of pay for stenographers on the sessional staff is much higher than the rate of pay prevailing in the service. This higher rate is paid because it is thoroughly understood that they must take the chance of the session being irregular and accept the possibility of being laid off between sessions. The sessional staff is not employed on the same conditions as permanent civil servants. It is paid by the day and its members are liable to be laid off when there is not sufficient work to justify their employment. Salaries are higher than in the government departments, but these employees must take the risk of being left unemployed during long adjournments or when a session is of short duration. They were not paid during the three-month adjournment from August 7 to November 5, 1940.
The matter of travelling expenses may possibly be raised, but the payment of such expenses to these employees is prohibited under the terms of standing order 89, which reads:
No allowance shall in future be made to any person in the employ of this house who may not reside at the scene of government, for travelling expenses in coming to attend his duties.
The members of the internal economy commission were unanimously of the opinion that whatever the house might do, certainly the country would not approve under present-day conditions of an expenditure of nearly $80,000 which is not authorized and which has not been contemplated.

Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, may I voice a protest, which is only my own but which may be shared by other members of the house, against this way of dealing with adjournments. We have examples that we should follow. We have one example in particular that is very good, and much better than any suggestions that may be offered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). It is the example of the province of Quebec. The premier of the province will attend the dominion-provincial conference in the middle of January notwithstanding the fact that the Quebec legislature is meeting on January 7. It was a notice sent by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in August, 1896, to every Liberal member,, telling him it was his duty to attend the opening of the first session after the general election; and I assume that that practice was followed for some years afterwards. This year we met without notice to any individual member. Members were notified by an announcement in the press. I do not think that is the right way to deal with members of parliament. When we adjourn and go home I think we should be summoned here on some other authority than that of the press. speechtext:
Before the question is put, I might be allowed to speak of one or two matters which have been referred to.
First of all, may I say to my hon. friend (Mr. Pouliot) who has just taken his seat that I have tried at all times as far as I could to be courteous towards hon. members with respect to matters pertaining to the sessions of parliament, as well as all else. I do not know whether that courtesy should be expected to go to the length of obliging me to write a personal letter to each hon. member in order to tell him that it is his duty to be in the house at the first meeting of a session.
My hon. friend referred to a letter which Sir Wilfrid Laurier wrote in 1896 to members of parliament. I believe I have seen a copy of that letter, and I think I know its purpose. Sir Wilfrid Laurier had just been returned to power. His government had come into office and was about to meet parliament for the first time, and Sir Wilfrid was anxious

Long Adjournment-Sessional Employees
to have all members of his party present so as to confer with them at the beginning of a new parliament, just as, I think, my hon. friend opposite did this year at the beginning of the present session; he had a party caucus at the beginning of the session with a view of greeting and meeting the members of his party. I do not believe that the letter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was ever intended by him as an official notice of the obligation upon members to attend the sittings of parliament. The official notice is given by proclamation. I should feel that I was belittling the intelligence of hon. members were I to take it upon myself to send to each of them a letter indicating what their duty was in the matter of attendance. I make that clear because I should not like to have it thought that I was discourteous, least of all to my hon. friend, because I know what would follow if I were.
May I say to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who has spoken about the sessional employees, that, while my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has given the house the information which it was necessary to give, the government naturally will wish, for example, as he suggested, in connection with the dominion-provincial conference, to make use of some of those who would not be employed at the time in the work of the Commons, and who might be of service when the conference is held. More than that I do not think I can say as to the position of the sessional staff.
I might mention, however, what I said to the hon. member for Davenport when he took up this matter with me privately. All over this country to-day are persons who are pressing to get any kind of government appointment, even for a few weeks. There is something of security-and that not any false sense of security-which belongs to those who were taken on at the beginning of the session and have been given to understand that they will be reappointed when the session continues. They are in a rather privileged position as matters stand at the present time.
My hon friend the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) has spoken about sessions of parliament being for the purpose not of making speeches but of enacting legislation. I agree with him that the purpose is not that of making speeches, particularly speeches which have nothing to do with our war effort. I believe that is an aspect with respect to speeches which we should keep very much in mind at the present time, if we do not, I am inclined to believe that the public will judge us critically. No one can realize how very serious the situation of the world is to-day and not feel that everything else is comparatively
14873-44 j
irrelevant: I say "comparatively", in relation to the importance of this House of Commons and this parliament concentrating thought and effort upon matters relating to the war. I am not stating anything which is not wholly obvious when I venture to say, it is not the quantity of talk, it is the quality of the decisions reached which counts in all that parliament does. I do not think it is a sign of high intelligence that a long time is needed in discussion in order to reach a decision. It seems to me that most persons who are able to reach decisions promptly do so usually because they have already become pretty fully informed upon the subject matter with which they are dealing. One does not need to restrict, one's opportunity to parliament in order to become informed with regard to most matters which are discussed here.
While I am speaking I should like to say a word about the view which has been so frequently expressed, that parliament should be continuously in session during the period of the war. I suppose every hon. member will agree that the parliament of the United Kingdom has a very much larger obligation, in matters of legislation, of war effort, and all else, than has this parliament of Canada. It has to legislate with respect not only to matters pertaining to the United Kingdom but also to those which relate to the large colonial empire and the empire of India. In addition it has the obligation of considering and deciding upon those classes of questions which in our country are considered by the nine provincial governments as well as the federal government. I mention these things because I believe it is helpful to have a true sense of proportion when we estimate the length of time necessary for discussion in the house as compared with such time as may be needed by the executive in order to carry out the policies which are decided upon here and the enactments that are passed.
I have had an estimate made of the length of time that the House of Commons in the United Kingdom parliament has sat since the beginning of the war. The period I have taken is the first year of war, that is to say, from the 1st of September, 1939, until August 31, 1940. I find that the sittings of the commons amount to 149 days. That represents 30 weeks of five days a week. It represents the entire period in number of days during which the commons have been in session in the British parliament in that period of time.
May I point out something else the significance of which I would ask hon. members to note. In the British House of Commons, in order that the ministers may be able
684	COMMONS
Long Adjournment-Sessional Employees
to discharge the heavy obligations that rest upon them at this time of war, parliament for the most part sits only three days in the week, not as we do, from Monday to Friday. The custom has been for the Prime Minister to indicate the days on which parliament shall sit, and after a careful survey of the British Hansard I find that both the late Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Churchill, while they did not make a definite rule-because sometimes they might wish to meet on Monday and at other times on Friday-generally moved that, when the house adjourned on Thursday night, it should stand adjourned until the following Tuesday. That obviously would not be workable in Canada where hon. members have to travel such great distances. What I do wish to point out, however, is that the British parliament, with all its heavy obligations, has found it possible to limit the time of its sittings as indicated, and also has found it necessary to follow the practice I have indicated because of the exceptional burden which of necessity is thrown upon a ministry during a time of war.
I would point out further that so far as the government of the United Kingdom is concerned, as hon. members are aware, the cabinet is only a part of the ministry. The ministry itself is a much larger body and it has supporting it many of the most highly trained minds of the United Kingdom, a very large staff of exceptionally well-informed experts. In our public service we are fortunate in many of our departments in having officials who are well qualified to give the very best expert advice, but for ministers to have a chance even to confer with the members of their staffs at a time like this, and to do so in any careful detail, requires time and opportunity. If parliament, when we resume, is to go on sitting from Monday to Friday, I think we shall have seriously to consider at that time how we can make a division of labour which will at least afford more opportunity than has thus far been available, to enable the ministry in this time of war to deal with the pressing problems which arise not only from day to day but from hour to hour, and to have longer periods of time for cabinet consultation and conference.
While I am on this subject, may I remind hon. members of the difference between our system of government and that of the United States. Every now and then one hears it said that President Roosevelt is able to do this and that, that he is able to broadcast, to travel, and so on. He and his ministers are able to do this, it is said; why, therefore cannot the same be done in Canada? Well, under the constitution of the United States the ministers have no immediate obligation

to congress. The president and his ministers, the secretaries of state, give their whole time to executive work and to submission of recommendations to congress. But so far as what would correspond to our parliament is concerned, either in the senate or in the house of representatives, they have no obligations beyond that of the president to appear occasionally before congress and the secretaries of state at particular times before committees.
I mention these facts only in order to help to make clear, not only to hon. members of this house but to the country generally, the position as it is in reality. If we consider the length of time necessarily spent by the ministry in Canada in dealing with questions of legislation and matters pertaining to their executive duties, and compare the position here with what it is either in the United States or in Great Britain, I think we shall find the comparison, from the point of view of the length of time accorded the ministry to fulfil its administrative obligations, more favourable to the executive in the United Kingdom and in the United States than it is in Canada.
Motion agreed to.

On the orders of the day:
Mr. H. R. FLEMING (Humboldt); I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). What arrangements are being made to speed up payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ARRANGEMENTS FOR DEALING WITH APPLICATIONS AND MAKING PAYMENTS
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind
enough to give me a copy of the question before I came in, and I have had the following answer prepared:
Regulations under order in council P.C. 3887, dated August 13, 1940, provided that applications for assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be submitted prior to the fifteenth of September and be supported by such information with respect to the average yield of wheat in the township or other area as may be available.
Applications were received from a large number of municipalities for all three provinces, and, of the townships for which applications were received, 1,950 were found to have a yield of thirteen bushels or less according to standing crop and stook-thresher estimates made by field inspectors.
These 1,950 townships were again visited by field inspectors to check acreage reports submitted by farmers, to determine farms on which the average yield of wheat is in excess of eight bushels per acre and on which the

Nickel and Scrap Iron
production of wheat is in excess of three thousand bushels and to obtain complete information with respect to township yields and farmers' status for the board of review.
The board of review began the examination of reports on November 4 and dealt with two-thirds of the applications received. Complete information was not available for the other townships; further reports have since been received and the board reconvened on December 2.
An emergency year was declared by order in council P.C. 6650 on November 20, 1940.
Because of delays in a number of townships for which complete information is still not available and difficulties in transportation conditions, it has not yet been possible to determine the exact number of townships which may be included in the crop failure category but it is expected that this can be done within the next few days.
Many applications have been received since September 15 for both township assistance and area substitution. It may be possible to deal with some of these under the regulations, but others will have to be rejected.
A large number of schedules for different townships have been completed and it is expected that the issuing and mailing of cheques will commence within the next few days.
It should be possible to have cheques for first payments under the act mailed to the great majority of those who will be eligible to receive them during December but it is not believed that this can be done in all cases.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OP DR. ROBERT MCCLURE AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OP DR. ROBERT MCCLURE AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext: In view of the statement made by Doctor Robert McClure, International Red Cross Director for China, speaking in Toronto last night, to the effect that " only last week a shipment of nickel was sent to Japan and will soon be found in the bodies of British soldiers," will the Prime Minister tell the house whether or not nickel is still being shipped to Japan, and secondly will he give some assurance to the house that this shameful traffic will be stopped?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT OP DR. ROBERT MCCLURE AS TO SHIPMENTS TO JAPAN
speechtext:
My hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of his question, and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) also came around with a similar notice with respect to this matter.
Let me say at once that no nickel has been shipped to Japan, as far as the government is aware, since the beginning of this year. My hon. friend speaks of an assurance. That assurance was given at the beginning of this session; not in the words which have been used by the hon. member, regarding a " shameful traffic," but an assurance that no permits would be granted for the export of nickel to Japan at this time, for reasons which were made quite clear in the statement.
I should like to take advantage of the question which my hon. friend has asked to read to the house the full report of what was said last night by the gentleman to whom the hon. member has referred, and I would ask hon. members to consider while I am reading it whether they feel that any responsibility is to be attached to utterances which are expressed in language such as appears in this speech, and also whether or not utterances of the kind are not very dangerous at a time like the present.
The dispatch which appeared in this morning's Ottawa Citizen, and I assume in the other newspapers as well, is dated Toronto, December 4, and is as follows:
Dr. Robert McClure, International Red Cross director for China, said in an address here to-night that Canadian nickel was being shipped to Japan as recently as last week "and I expect some one will soon be digging it out of British bodies."
He said the reason is that "Canadian merchants want the profit."
"For three years I have been digging Canadian scrap iron out of Chinese bodies and I expect someone will soon be digging it out of British bodies, for Japan is now ready to attack Singapore. That is all her build-up in French Indo-China means. ..."
I want to repudiate a statement of that kind just as strongly as it is possible to do so. 1 cannot understand how anyone holding any kind of responsible position could allow himself to use words of the kind in regard to a situation so delicate as is the present international situation.
I saw this report this morning. A telegram was sent immediately to Doctor McClure by the under-secretary of state for external affairs. When a reply is received I shall be pleased to give it either to the house or to the press. The telegram was as follows:
Canadian Press despatch in this morning's Ottawa Citizen quotes you as saying in an address in Toronto that Canadian nickel was being shipped to Japan as recently as last week. No nickel can be exported from Canada without a permit, and no permit has been granted for export to Japan since January 2nd, 1940. If you have any evidence of specific illegal shipment please communicate it at once so that the government may institute necessary investigations with view to prosecution. If you have not please correct Canadian Press report for publication.
Trade Agreements-Bacon

Perhaps I might be permitted to add a word in reference to the export of scrap iron, since scrap iron was also mentioned by Doctor McClure. I stated to the house at the beginning of the session, and I repeat now, that no permits have been issued for the export of scrap iron to Japan since the autumn of last year.

speechtext:
ing and for all orders in council on soldier matters. Apparently we are carrying on a Liberal war, because no return was ever made; apparently some official stopped it. We now have this budget which provides funds, first, for conscription for home defence and, second, in order to protect the neutrality of the United States. All the money collected by this new budget should be spent upon the battle of Britain and the battle of the Mediterranean before it is too late. We have been too late in everything.
I should like to say to the Prime Minister, who is not in the chamber at the moment, that I challenge every statement he made in this house the day before yesterday about our war effort and about things looking brighter. I make the same challenge as was made in New Zealand and Australia when recruiting was stepped up. The money raised by this budget should be spent for war purposes and the taxpayers of this country should not be taxed the way they are for non-essentials and so-called luxuries. Our primary object should be to help the mother country. As I said before, this budget is of more importance than the main budget which will be brought down next year. It contains two cardinal principles. First, the government wants to increase all production and, second, the government wants to restrict consumption, both private and public, as much as possible.
The man on the street wants to know about this budget and the debates in this house. He does not object to paying taxes if they are used for the defence of civilization, freedom and religion, in the battle of Britain, but he does object to paying taxes for things that are of secondary importance, such as home defence, and many other useless expenditures, for example, on the old league; a new one, pan-Americanism; collective security and pacifist doctrines. The House of Commons is the only forum where a person can have his grievances dealt with and learn the facts. The man on the street does object to his grievances not being ventilated, and he does object to the press not giving some report of what goes on in the House of Commons, because he desires to learn what the ^ policy of the government is, what a minister proposes, and what is proposed by the official opposition and by the hon. gentlemen of the two groups to my left on the other side of the budget debate.
I have no bouquets to throw at the government, because I am greatly dissatisfied with the war effort of the government, both before and since the war started. Down to the hour of the outbreak of war they had done nothing but support neutrality and disarmament. For four or five years in this house I have been

urging rearmament. I did not wait for the war to start to urge that a rearmament budget be brought down. For the past five years I have forgotten politics and have worked in and out of the house to arouse the country from its apathy to the proper need for security and preparation. I have not made speeches as far apart and different as the poles and a right-about face. I have been a consistent supporter of the rearmament policy of the government since they started to take up this work.
One of the main things to which I object in this budget-and this is the second we have had; the minister should be able to combine them in one-is that we have nothing to relieve real estate or the municipalities, whose revenues have been taken away. Instead, the government is making up its budget with an income tax, an excess profits tax, and all these federal burdens which are placed upon the municipalities, with resulting overgovernment and overtaxation, and appropriating municipal revenues such as income tax and other taxes. We have no redress in this respect. Another thing I object to is the unfair way in which, in connection with the Municipal Assistance Act, the money provided for relief and relief works has been distributed. Ontario got nothing.
After the collapse of France, Mr. Churchill said, regarding the budget, that members of parliament should " search their own consciences, as I frequently search mine," because everybody has made mistakes. It seems to me, in looking at both the amendment and the subamendment, that the only use in recriminating about the past is to enforce effective action at the present. We seem to have done everything too late. As I see it, panic has stimulated the government to action. Britain and France learned to their sorrow from bitter experience that constructive criticism prevents governments from reacting into blunders which are nothing but suicide. So long as criticism is honest, founded on facts and not inspired by any ulterior political motive, it is more helpful, urgent and necessary in war time than in peace.
With reference to this particular debate on the budget and what it is for, and the conduct of the war, we seem to be too late in everything. We were too late in getting this long deferred relief to the mother country and helping her to bear the burden. Nine times out of ten we have been too late-too late in recruiting; too late in our operations respecting the Bren gun and bombing planes; too late in the commonwealth air training scheme; too late in respect of clothing, boots and equipment; too late in furnishing money for

War Budget-Mr. Church
dependents; too late in supplying big guns, mine sweepers, bombers, real tanks, Bren guns, and modern rifles and munitions; too late in dealing with the fifth column; too late getting a survey of industrial and economic power; too late in organizing large and small plants for the manufacture of munitions, torpedo boats, and aircraft such as Spitfires; too late in preventing the menace which arises from magazines printed in the United States, which have exhibited Anglo-phobia for years, and from United States radio programmes which are sent into Canada every day to destroy the morale of the Canadian people. Help Britain now; argue about it afterwards. It is now or never, now and forever in this hour of need.
In connection with this ways and means committee, I would say to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who has recently returned from England, that I am glad to see the government has given, by way of reduced rates, a small concession to the mother country, situated as she is; but if it had been done in 1938 or 1939 it would have been much better. Away back in 1938 I urged upon the Minister of Agriculture that he should establish food reservoirs over in England, that he should send the exportable surplus of grain to be stored over there, in addition to bacon, canned goods and other foodstuffs, because of grave submarine menace, such as we experienced in the last war.
When we saw the disaster coming, I put forward the constructive suggestion that Canada should find a way of making possible the impossible. In other words, where there were no barracks or implements of war we should do as we did before, namely, take other public buildings. I said, if men have no uniforms, let them train without uniforms. If they have no rifles, machine guns or other modern implements of warfare, let them do as had been done in France and Great Britain, namely, use dummies until the real weapons can be obtained. Instead of allowing these men to drift round with nothing to do, they should be given the proper training immediately. Canada misjudged the whole situation. I said in 1938 it would take two years to train men and two years to get any real munitions.
If the government needs money it must, no doubt, go the easiest way to secure it in order to finance the war, but what I object to is the way they are doing it. In my opinion the government should charge seventy per cent of this war expenditure, if of primary importance, not secondary, to capital, and about thirty per cent to income. Industry
cannot continue any longer to carry the burdens, restraints and all these artificial barriers which are placed upon it by a score of boards. I do not know how businessmen are going to conduct their operations or businesses, with all the boards which have been appointed in this country. We are simply being headed for state socialism all along the line, and the rank of a totalitarian state, and nobody will want to conduct a business or have one, with the artificial barriers and burdens which are being imposed and the attitude expressed by the leader of the group on my left, with regard to conscription of industry and all wealth. The municipalities are starved by federal and provincial powers grabbing their revenues, and the time is coming when they will have no money with which to carry out some of their functions, with those imposed by Ottawa on them. There was established by the British North America Act in this country overgovernment and overtaxation by a duplicate municipal system, resulting in a triple-header system of taxation, with dominion, provincial and municipal budgets, so much so, with the increased income tax and the added sales tax on civic utilities and all this kind of thing, that the time has come when the minister should consider more carefully my proposal to assess two-thirds of the amount in the ways and means resolution to capital, and the balance to revenue.
Hon. gentlemen of the social credit party believe that the way to raise this money is not by taxes and borrowing, but by inflation, namely, to start the printing-press, create paper money by a gamble, and let the government use it for war purposes. We are told that the amount required next war year will be about a billion dollars. But now the social credit party abandon all that and their principles and support the amendment moved by the leader of the other group.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment goes further than the social credit proposals. If we accept the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation proposal to reconstruct industry, trade and commerce and our financial institutions in war time and conscript industry and wealth, we are going to kill all our war effort, supported by the majority of the people of the industrial provinces, who pay eighty per cent of the taxes under this budget. I believe the sense of the people of the two central provinces is opposed to any such drastic change at the present time as unwise and uneconomic. It would dislocate industry, which is already severely handicapped by these artificial barriers and burdens, and crushing loads which
War Budget-Mr, Church

are placed on business to-day. We are fast approaching a totalitarian state, with these numerous excursions into state socialism, with the main budget and this baby budget, as it is called, with sickness and unemployment insurance-which I have supported.
What have we to-day? The business man is so taxed that he is taxed to death. One of the glories of the Victorian era was that the people kept the state. Now the state keeps the people, and we are squandering our resources in the directions indicated by such an amendment as is proposed here, many of them with regard to non-essentials. In England the Socialist party, as I pointed out the other day, did everything they could before the war to defeat the government in any plan for rearmament. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, in this amendment, do not attack sound money as a principle; but, as far as I can see, claim that the whole organization of industry is on a wrong basis and that all war production should be on a socialistic basis.
To beat Hitler, the minister says, we shall have to increase our production by greater efficiency. I believe the time is coming when we should, in this budget, cut out the nonessentials, such as roads to Alaska, uneconomic duplication in roads, legations, league votes and so forth. We are collecting too much money from the people for purposes which are of no value in the prosecution of this war.
Britain has always been able to protect Canada and has never failed us. We owe to her our peace here, free from invasion. There is a great deal of talk about Canada and the joint defence board. There are too many speeches for which Hitler cares nothing. Canada cannot be talked out of the British empire by those who want a political union, and pacifists and pan-Americans. The defence board is all board and no defence so far, from what I see of it, and if it is for this that we are taxing the people in this budget we could use the money better elsewhere, because the battle of Britain is primary and this is secondary. Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire. Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire. If Canada could have been talked out of the British empire, it would have been talked out of it long ago by some of the theories which have been proposed in and out of this house.
Canada was not ready when this war came. For four years the government had been listening to the babble of the pacifists and isolationists, and we had a foreign policy based on complacency. The government refused to see the handwriting on the wall and did nothing. They misjudged the whole European situation.

I come now to the celebrated victory loan of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and I should like to have his attention for a moment, also that of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Hoblitzell), who is at present sitting beside him. I am one of the constituents of the hon. member for Eglinton. He is a great sportsman and all that, but I think he would do well to hearken to his constituents for whom I have been speaking this afternoon. I have referred to the working classes that live there. Many of them come from various parts of Ontario, and very few of them, on account of the taxes and burdens on real estate, could subscribe to the victory loan. The brass-band method was used to raise this last loan, but the people were scared off it by all this talk about belt-tightening and heavy taxes to come, and this talk of a joint defence board, and that we should pay attention only to home defence, when the people knew well that Britain had been left to fight the battle of civilization all by herself, without any allies, and that it was to her we owed our freedom. Is it any wonder that the victory loan did not go over well, because it was ill-timed, when the people were burdened with all the taxes I have mentioned, when there is confiscation of property in many cities and even in the riding of Eglinton owing to federal and provincial authorities having refused to lighten the burden on real estate, with all these federal taxes, which amount to nearly five or six mills on the dollar in Toronto and other municipal tax rates. Many of the people of Eglinton riding and of all Toronto industrial ridings generally are losing their property because of the heavy taxation, federal and provincial, placed on municipal institutions, and this parliament and the Minister of Finance hold out no hope of relief. Yet the minister tells the real estate people to tighten their belts and continue to pay for relief works and many other duplicate forms of taxation.
The second victory loan was put on at the wrong time. It was poorly advertised. The government paid 1| to li points too much for this loan last September, and that is going to be reflected in the country's tax rate. I have had some experience with large loans, with the $32,000,000 deal, for instance, to take over the power companies in the Niagara Falls district, also, while I was in office, for almost seven years, in connection with the $200,000,000 bond transaction re municipal utilities when we took over the Toronto Street Railway and harbour, and power and light matters. I can tell you this, that if we had adopted the methods used by the government in the first and second victory loans we would never have been able to pay the rates, or to have paid what was asked in 1913 for some of these prop-

War Budget-Mr. Church
erties. See what happens next year! Notwithstanding all the taxes in this special budget and the taxes that will be brought down in the budget next spring, the minister now announces a new victory loan for next summer, and frightens the people with a scarecrow programme, because that is all it is. He is going to scare off all the investors by all this belt-tightening talk. Belt-tightening on what? Is it to be belt-tightening of the kind urged by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, the conscription of the money that a man has left in his pocket? All these taxes, the income tax, excess profits tax, foreign exchange tax and all the rest, loading up real estate with a burden that it cannot carry, are bound to have an effect when we go to the country for another loan next summer with all this overgovemment and overtaxation.
I	congratulate the	leader of	this	party(Mr. Hanson)	upon	the speech	he	madein	the house	yesterday. He,	has	neverfaltered in his love of Britain despite the attacks which have been made upon him for his speech at Charlottetown. What he	said there	was	quite correct.	The
Ogdensburg agreement has been referred to by other speakers. It was a talk, not an agreement, all right in its way as it is of tremendous importance to have the United States with us, but that talk was exactly the same as the government's 1938-39 defence policy, of home defence, and the second cardinal principle is to protect our neutrality if the United States is attacked. There was much ado about nothing over that Ogdensburg agreement, but Canada's defence policy had the same cardinal principles. I agree with what the leader of this party said yesterday on our tariff policy and the need of protecting Canadian industry and agriculture.
This government changed the Ottawa agreements, and all hon. members know what happened. This government gave the United States almost the same advantages that we enjoy in the Ottawa agreements. We had a 6 cent preference in the British market on grain carried in British ships, and generally the Ottawa agreements were the backbone of the prosperity that we had before the war on bacon and other products. Our trade with Britain increased by 44 per cent and Britain's trade with us by 42 per cent under them. The resolutions now before us to aid Britain were a wise gesture. Britain is protecting our shores, and if the government will only consult with industry, labour and agriculture I believe that we can reduce import duties against Britain 50 per cent more on some goods in certain items and 100 per cent more in other lines. That is, if those reductions
can be made without hurting labour and industry in Canada. The British fleet and the Royal Air Force are the real Monroe doctrine and not a mythical Monroe doctrine as expressed in a joint defence board, which without Britain is a myth. The Monroe doctrine for the United States and us is the British fleet and the Royal Air Force, and that is why at Christmas our country and the United States will not be invaded, for which the United States should give thanks by aiding Britain. I hope that conferences will be held by the government with industry, labour and agriculture to see if our imports from Great Britain cannot be extended all along the line in order to help out the mother country when she has so few friends, and has lost most of her export trade, if Canada is not injured in doing what I suggest.
I believe there should be an exemption granted with respect to some of the provisions relating to exchange. Why should United States citizens and British subjects have to go to all this trouble to send some poor relative a present of $25 or $50? Why should a man who wants to send $10 or $15 to a relative in the United States who may need it to pay a hospital bill have to go through all this red tape and formula of the foreign exchange control board with all its standing army of officials? From 1921 to 1930, under our pan-American tariff 600,000 of our citizens left Canada to go to the United States to look for a job, and many of them were soldiers who fought in the great war, and some of them are fighting in this war, at great hazard to their lives. Why should they be hampered up to the amount I name, by the foreign exchange control board when they had to leave this country to look for jobs betwen 1921 and 1930?
Another thing is the passport plague. Is this the Monroe doctrine in action? Also, cannot it be amended before Christmas, and what is being done? Neither country benefits from such drastic measures.
I would also repeal a lot of this Canada-United States trade agreement. It was for three years, and expires in 1940. It was to the disadvantage of Britain and Canada, and my hon. leader gave many illustrations of that yesterday. How can we compete with these people with such adverse trade treaties against agriculture and industry in Canada? They are our friends and kinsmen and it is of the greatest importance that we should try to maintain most warm and amicable relations with them forever. No one has ever suggested anything else. They are our friends to-day, and long may they continue to be. But business is business. If it is looked upon as a matter of pure business in dealing with the mother
War Budget-Mr. Church

country that we should consider ourselves in trade, why should it not be business when we are dealing with another competing country? Why should we give away our market, taking work away from our own workmen and giving it to our competitors across the border, and our own markets with exchange as it is?
A few years ago I brought up the question of a national coal supply for Canada. The minister could conserve a great deal of exchange by adopting a national coal supply policy such as was urged in 1922 and 1923. The importation of bituminous coal free of duty may not be detrimental to Canada as a whole but it may be to Nova Scotia. It was the coal from the maritime provinces and Alberta and Wales that I had in view when I proposed a national, all-British coal supply policy in 1922, and it took ten years to get it recognized. If the maritime provinces suffer by the new free British duties here, they should be given increased protection by way of bonuses, subventions and subsidies so that the interests of those provinces should not be injured.
As regards cotton, woollens and fabrics of all kinds, I submit that the government ought to confer with industry and labour to see if something cannot be done to lighten the burden on the mother country, especially when she has lost her export trade. For fifteen years I have been asking this question: Why are there so many Washington-made tariffs? Largely as a result of the abrogation of the Ottawa agreement, Washington has become the economic capital of the British empire. There is a right and a wrong way of securing concessions from the United States. If they were convinced that we were losing all this money, I believe they would be the first to take steps to bring about some change in our favour with regard to tariff reform.
I am opposed to the price-fixing theory. As regards railway fares, it is all right for the railways to get out hand-bills quoting fares of $30, $35 and $40 from Halifax to Toronto, but as a matter of fact we find very low excursion rates. For instance, there was an excursion on November 28, the fare being $17.50 to Truro. Other figures to points in the maritime provinces were $16.25, $15, $17 and $18. Yet, when the poor soldiers want transportation they cannot get it and are refused a $20 return rate from Truro. We have spent millions of dollars on the Canadian National railway, and this will have to be taken into account in the budget, because the taxpayers will have to pay the deficit on our railways. Yet they cannot carry soldiers free. But although the railways can give all kinds of excursion rates every week to civilians, when it comes to railway fares for our soldiers in 
Ontario they quote higher, fabulous rates to maritime places.
The government has done nothing about insurance for soldiers. I have asked about four or five times what it intends to do in this regard. The minister said that the superintendent of insurance had written a letter. He did in the session of 1939 and that was the last I heard from him.
Again, the government should bring down a policy with regard to grain. The people of the industrial provinces can no longer pay such extended annual bonuses, subventions and the cost of pegging grain. They cannot afford the measures brought down almost at every session. The industrial workers and the farmers of the three central provinces and of the maritimes get little or nothing in return in bonuses and subventions. It is of the utmost importance that the grain industry should be on a good basis and receive all due assistance, but there has been a serious want of judgment in marketing the crop in war time. The government misjudged the markets. They failed to establish English reservoirs; they failed to cooperate with the department of agriculture at Washington on the question of the wider marketing of grain during the war, with the loss of ships which we are sustaining at the present time.
I am opposed to any new pan-American league of nations of north and south America because I believe it will lead to the same state of affairs as has developed in Europe, and to more strife than peace. I am opposed to any proposal to link up this country with any more such pan-American alliances over the head of this parliament, and without our knowledge, and I suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that in the recess he should find out all the circumstances relating to the disaster that has overtaken seventeen of our merchant ships off the west coast of Ireland on the way to England from Canada. The cost of that disaster will be reflected in the coming budget next spring and in lost trade, lives, and goods. Will the government make an inquiry into this matter? Will the Prime Minister find out whether these neutral ports and inlets are being used against Canada and Canadian trade, and whether they shelter German submarines? Many businessmen are losing consignments on these ships and they will be without any compensation and will want a show-down. I urge, therefore, that during the recess the government take steps to ascertain what is being done to protect Canadian interests in relation to the question of neutrality in this area. I raised this question on July 10 last.
Parliament is going to have a holiday for more than two months. We are going to take

a holiday until February 17, and yet the government cannot give a brief holiday to our soldiers, or even a day to the men in our air force. These men are fighting for civilization, for religion, for Christianity; and yet on the greatest of religious holidays, Christmas day, Canadian soldiers of the Royal Canadian Air Force are to be denied leave to visit their parents and friends. I suggest to the government that if they want to hurt recruiting they should continue as they are doing in this respect, in not aiding to the utmost our soldiers who risk their all for the country.

Concessions were made by reducing the tariff on their raw materials; I have no objection to that. Why were they so successful in the two years following the reduction? It is easy to see why. It was for the simple reason that prices went down and people bought automobiles more freely, and although the manufacturers had to accept a smaller profit on each automobile, their aggregate profits at the end of the year showed a large increase. After all, what is the secret of success in any line of merchandising? Is it to sell one article a day and make fifty cents profit on the sale, or is it to sell ten articles a day and make ten cents profit on each article? The more goods you sell the more profit you make and the more service you can give.
Here may I quote, with approval, the statement made by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman): "There has never in Canadian history been a tariff reduction which did not benefit Canadian manufacturers, but they fear it." Ah! Fear! Fear! That is it. Fear, which at one time was no doubt the natural and normal reaction of man in his primitive state and was intended as a necessary shield for his self-preservation, has to-day become a heavy and burdensome armour, impeding him in his upward march towards a higher civilization. That fear which in those days was a physical, bodily fear, and quite normal, has to-day become simply an atavic, mental and moral fear-the curse of humanity, and man's greatest enemy.
If I were-I was going to say if I were king, but I will put it in a more modern way- if I were the dictator of Canada, do you know what I would do, Mr. Speaker? I would issue a decree to take effect to-morrow morning, establishing absolute free trade in this country.

I am sure the Minister of Finance would be the last to deny that had it not been for the vision of that man and his knowledge of finance and monetary problems, we should not have been so well equipped as we are to-day to deal with what to me is an abstruse and technical matter.
I will admit that the former leader of the Conservative party had something like vision, but it was more than that, he had visions. We may differ sometimes, but we are still patriotic. Our diuty is not to follow blindly the lead of the government in this matter, our duty is to warn the government against the danger of certain tariff policies in order that the people of Canada may not suffer either in the near future or later on. No one should be depressed at the present time; we should ail have courage; we should have what Mr. Bennett called "fortitude," during this present war.
We should endeavour to pass legislation which will not prove a handicap to Canadian business during the war and afterwards. Tariff changes are very delicate matters. It would be easy for one of these clever boys who act as pages here to go through the Canadian tariff with a blue pencil and strike out certain items and change others, and then present them as a budget. We should not forget that many people are employed by the importers of Canada. If we destroy the import trade, these importers will be put completely out of business. If the mission of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) to south America is a wise move, as I think it is, then we should not isolate ourselves with high tariffs. Not only did I fight this type of legislation when Mr. Bennett was leading the government, I tried to do what I could to prevent it from being put into force when our own party was in power.
I was much concerned over the fact that those who had been the advisers of Mr. Bennett were also acting as advisers to the then Minister of Finance. They were considered as experts and their word was powerful. But I did something else. I was concerned over the financial disaster which had been brought about by the brain trust in the United States, and therefore the member for Temis-couata moved to introduce a bill to repeal the act which had established an economic council. The first reading of this bill was on February 24, 1936, at which time I said1, as reported on page 437 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, it is very easy to explain the purpose of this bill. It is to put the axe of parliamentary control to a dry branch of the dead tree of so-called social legislation.

I had quite strong support in introducing that bill. A few days later, when the second reading was up on February 27, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, as reported at page 578 of Hansard:
Mr. Mackenzie King: The measure comes under the Prime Minister. The act provides for the appointment of an economic council to advise the Prime Minister. I am quite satisfied with my own council; I do not think I need an economic council to tell the present government what is necessary in the way of legislation. The government at all times is in a position to command the services .of any members of the public service. It seems to me wholly superfluous to have on the statute book a law which obligates the government to bring together a number of the members of the public service and constitute them into an advisory council, when members of _ the public service have enough to do in their own departments if they are doing their work properly.
That was very well said.
It is prodigal to add to public expenditures to the extent necessitated by this act. I think the government made its attitude toward the legislation clear when we did not place in the estimates an appropriation for the legislation, and I do not think it is necessary for us to say anything more about it. It is superfluous legislation, and our attitude towards it when the late government introduced the measure was that it was superfluous. However, being a part of the new deal which was being tried out it was allowed to pass. The public has since expressed its view with respect to much of the late government's legislation and made clear its attitude towards some of these measures. The present government does not feel it in the public interest to continue the legislation.

I have nothing against these fellows. The government may pay them any amount they wish in the way of salaries provided these men do not give any advice. I fear for the future of this country if all these people are giving advice to the government. Mr. PERCY C. BLACK (Cumberland): Mr. Speaker, all the people of Canada are interested in the resolutions submitted to this house by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). Nova Scotia has a particular interest in one item, namely, the admission into Canada from Great Britain of bituminous coal duty free. If this means anything, it must mean that a large additional import of coal and other commodities is to be made. Otherwise there is no necessity for the resolutions.
I understand that in recent weeks there has been imported from Great Britain 2,000,000 tons of bituminous coal, most of which is now in storage for the Montreal-St. Lawrence market. If the change in the duty is to have the effect it is supposed to have and there is to be a large additional importation of bituminous coal, it means the displacement of Nova Scotia coal in the markets that have been recognized as belonging to Nova Scotia; that is, the maritime provinces, Quebec, and eastern Ontario as far west as is necessary to absorb sufficient coal to take up the production of Nova Scotia.

If Great Britain is to be put in a position to pay, at least in part, for her enormous importations, she must be allowed to export to this country and to the United States-a privilege she was denied by the United States in making payments on the loans in the last war.
If taking off the duty on bituminous coal means anything, it means that a large quantity of bituminous coal will come into the Canadian markets to which I have referred, to the disadvantage of Nova Scotia. I should like it. to be understood that if that is to be done-and I am not going to oppose it-then subventions and assistance should be extended so that Nova Scotia coal can be marketed to

points farther west in Ontario in order that the total output of Nova Scotia coal may be absorbed in Canada. We in Nova Scotia treasure very highly the subventions and other assistance which have been given to coal mining during the last ten years. The importance of that assistance has been recognized, I believe, by all the people of Canada. It was put into effect when the coal trade of Nova Scotia was at the most difficult period in its existence. In
1930,	372,000 tons of Nova Scotia coal were assisted by subvention. In 1939 that amount was increased to 2,381,995 tons; in the ten months of the present fiscal year the total quantity so assisted is 1,828.000 tons. It is necessary that this assistance be rendered. Costs of production are higher than for imported coal; the men are entitled to a fair wage; and the people of Nova Scotia are entitled to this market, the only one open to them, that they may have fair treatment within confederation, and to some extent obtain the means whereby they can pay for their enormous purchases of commodities of many kinds from central Canada. Many of these commodities are mass-produced, and there is no possibility of manufacturing them in outlying portions of Canada.

As part of that policy the duty on bituminous coal was increased 50 per cent, to seventy-five cents a ton; a duty on anthracite coal of fifty cents a ton was put into effect, where there was no duty before; and a duty of $1 a ton was placed upon coke, thereby encouraging the production of coke in Canada, and a bonus of $1 a ton paid on Canadian coal used for coke. But these subventions have been entirely paid for through the increased
revenues accruing from the additional duties placed upon imported coal. For the last ten years the additional revenues have totalled $24,352,000. The total subventions paid to eastern and western Canada in the same period amounted to $21,333,000, so that a surplus of $3,000,000 accrued to the treasury of Canada over this period by virtue of this fuel policy. Furthermore, if it had not been put into effect, many of the coal mines of Nova Scotia could not have continued to operate. At that time they were in a desperate plight; in fact, the government of Nova Scotia had to plead with the banks that credit might be extended to tide this industry over that very, very difficult period.
I would mention particularly one man from central Canada who was most helpful to us in Nova Scotia at that time. I refer to the Hon. Wesley Gordon, then Minister of Mines and Labour, who cooperated with us on every occasion and assisted in increasing the duties and subventions. It meant tens of thousands of dollars in additional costs to the consumers of coal used in his constituency. On top of the other difficulties, he said it might result in such intense criticism of himself that he might never come back to the federal parliament. "But," he said, "I believe you are entitled to it and I am going to stand by you and put it into effect." He did, and I am grateful to Wesley Gordon and the Bennett government for what they did in those hard years in Canada and particularly in Nova Scotia from 1930 to 1933.
There is one other man whose name I would mention. He was really the author of the Canadian fuel-steel policy-the Hon. Gordon S. Harrington, deputy minister of national defence overseas in the last war, premier of Nova Scotia, and first chairman of the unemployment insurance board. He gave splendid service to the people of Nova Scotia and Canada in connection with coal and other matters. He regarded his duty to the public so highly that he refused a judgeship in that province-and there are very few men who have sat in this house who have refused such positions of great honour and trust in order to continue to serve in public life. I was sorry indeed that he was not given fuller justice last year when he was referred to by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), but we in Nova Scotia are under a great obligation to Colonel Harrington. He is out of politics now, but his work with regard to the fuel policy will be a lasting credit to him.

There has been much delay in equipping our soldiers. Last week-end I was motoring from Amherst to Oxford and Pugwash and I overtook a soldier. He was two hundred yards ahead of me when he beckoned me to stop. He wanted to get home to his family in Oxford. The temperature was almost zero; there were six inches of snow, and he had no overcoat. I asked him where his overcoat was and he said that none had been issued to him. I suggested that he must be an exception and he assured me that there were two hundred men in the North Nova Scotia Highlanders who had not yet been given greatcoats. It is hard to understand that. It seems strange, therefore, that there should be a lack of clothing for these men. It is said that the trainees are given their equipment more expeditiously and are given better equipment than the men who have enlisted for active service, the argument being that it will make a good impression at their camps and when they go home they will say how well they have been treated. Mr. Speaker, I have asked my people to have patience, and there has been very little criticism. The feeling, however, has been fairly definite and fairly widespread that everything possible has not been done and that fair consideration has not been given the people of Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces generally. I do not wish to be unduly critical, but I do not see how I can remain silent with respect to these matters that are of so much concern to the people whom I represent.
In his statement a few days ago the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) included a table showing the purchases by his department up to September 30, 1940. Total purchases in Canada amounted to $383,941,515. Of this total only $7,445,561 was spent in Nova Scotia, or less than two per cent. With

War Budget-Mr. Black (Cumberland)
many of our industries idle or working on part time this cannot help but create discontent. About November 20 I received a circular, as did all other hon. members, I presume, from the office of the director of public information, indicating that the Department of Munitions and Supply had placed orders for 120 sets of harness and twenty portable sawmills capable of sawing 20,000 feet of timber a day, for use by the forestry corps overseas. In my constituency we have a prominent harness factory, and at Oxford we have a manufacturer of portable sawmills. I assumed that these firms had been given an opportunity to tender for these materials, and if that had been so, I would have had no complaint. I communicated with them, and set out the information contained in this circular. I had a reply from A. E. Wry-Standard, Limited, one of the larger harness manufacturers, who market their products over Canada, stating that they had never had even an inquiry, that they did not know the material had been required and therefore could not submit their prices. I wrote the Oxford Foundry and Machine Company, Limited, at Oxford, Nova Scotia, and from that company I received this telegram:
Appreciate yours -of 21st instant. No inquiry or tender received for portion of twenty sawmills required for forestry corps for operation in Great Britain. We feel this discrimination against maritime province industries. Thanks for your very fine cooperation.
These two firms are listed in the Canadian Trade Index, which is put out by the Canadian Manufacturers Association and accepted all over Canada as authoritative. Under "harness" is listed A. E. Wry-Standard, Limited, one of twenty-five firms under this heading; under "sawmills, portable", is listed Oxford Foundry and Machine Company, Limited, together with fifteen other firms. The Oxford company makes a specialty of these sawmills, supplying practically the entire requirements of the maritime provinces and even shipping some of their mills to the United States. They have patented many devices or appliances in connection with their sawmills and have acquired the reputation of being one of the best manufacturers of sawmills in Canada. How can the people of Cumberland or of eastern Canada be content when firms such as these are not given even an opportunity to quote? If they had submitted their specifications and figures; if the specifications were not suitable or the prices were too high, I would have no complaints; but I do remonstrate when firms such as these-and they are only two of many-are not even given an opportunity to tender.
Many new industries are being established in Canada; I understand that many millions of dollars are being expended for this purpose. None of these industries is being established in the maritime provinces. There is also the Christie Trunk and Bag company, of Amherst. There was some publicity given to certain requirements in their line, but they were not given a chance to figure either. I do not wish to be too critical, I waited upon Colonel W. A. Harrison, an executive of the Department of Munitions and Supply early last summer, and he gave me the assurance that he would do what he could to see that some recognition was given the people of the maritime provinces. I know that in some instances that has been done, but in many others it has not.
We have other industries as well, such as the rolling mills at Amherst. Since I came to Ottawa I have received representations to the effect that the workmen there are anxious to do their part but that the mill is about to close down because it has no orders. There are also the salt mines at Malagash; with the need for large chemical plants in Canada in connection with our war undertaking, some special consideration might be given them and the industries of eastern Canada, such as those I have mentioned.
Protection was given to our industries back in 1878; in some instances bonuses were given in order that industries might be built up for peace-time service and be ready in case of an emergency such as we have at the present time. Never in the history of Canada, however, have grants been made to industries to the extent practised since the beginning of this war, and particularly in recent months. It is time some consideration is given to the outlying portions of Canada that have sacrificed a great deal in the interests of victory. How can we expect to have a united war effort in all Canada if consideration is not extended to those outlying parts of the country? Not only should industries be established for war purposes; they should be given assistance in order that they might have an opportunty of continuing operations in peace time. Then there would be better distribution of industry throughout Canada, but so far as I know that has not been done in connection with expenditures in the maritimes by this government.
Another question which I am sorry I have to bring up is in connection with the airport in Amherst. I do not wish to be critical, but in justice to the people whom I represent here I must make a statement. Aeroplanes have been assembled at Amherst. How do I know? Well, a report was made to parliament
