on May 21, 1940, covering the work being done in Canada, and in that report I find this paragraph:
Amherst:
The assembly of Anson wings and aircraft.
The overhaul of Anson aircraft.
Amherst was asked to provide the land for a runway first, then for a standard port and then for a super-standard port, and Amherst complied with every request. The town was then asked to go fifty-fifty on the cost of grading the land. The money could not be provided until the expenditure was submitted to the ratepayers, who approved more than one hundred in favour to every one who voted against it. The people of Amherst have a patriotic interest in this, and they have, too, a money interest. The Right Hon. Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of England, expressed the views of the English people when he said that never in history did so many people owe so much to so few. Our people want to be of assistance, and they want to have the undertakings implemented.
I do not blame the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). If I may judge from my contact with him, I would say that I am sure he wishes to get results. I do not blame Mr. Ralph Bell, who is in charge of aeroplane construction; knowing him as I do, I believe he, too, desires to get results. I did blame the Canadian Car and Foundry Company. I visited their plant at Montreal, and had a chance to see what they were doing. I doubt whether there is another firm in Canada that is doing better war work than this company. The people of Amherst are not at fault; so why have we not results? Someone is to blame. I am going to leave the matter there.
I am sorry the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is not at present in his seat. I understand he is overseas conferring with the British authorities. May I pay my respects to him, and tell him that the people of Amherst, of Cumberland, in fact the people of not only Nova Scotia but of all Canada, have confidence in him and are proud of what he is doing. At the time of the last war he did his work well, and I am satisfied he will do it to the limit of his ability in the present war.
I am pleased, too, to join with other hon. members in welcoming to the house my associate from Nova Scotia, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald). He is here only because duty has called him. Associated with me in this chamber are five of us who had experience together in the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia. That legislature has sent good men to this chamber and to the public life of Canada. From that legislature came Sir Charles Tupper,

Sir John Thompson, at one time Prime Minister of Canada; the Hon. W. S. Fielding, the Hon. A. K. Maclean, and many others I could mention.
The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services has said in the house that he is here to speak for those men who go down to the sea in ships and do business in great waters. He also has the traditions of the British navy to follow, the traditions of Drake, Nelson, Beatty and Churchill. Churchill with whom to some extent he will no doubt be associated, was First Lord of the Admiralty soon after the declaration of war. It was he who sent ships of the British navy to Norway, irrespective of international law. We remember the greeting they got there, "The navy is here!" That is the watchword all over the world-in South America, in Iceland, on the stormy Atlantic-everywhere: "The British navy is here!"
Therefore my hon. friend, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs has a great duty to perform and a great tradition to follow. He has to follow and be worthy of Mr. Churchill, that man of destiny, that man who, prior to 1939, was warning the British people, and who later became First Lord of the Admiralty. He was First Lord of the Admiralty at the beginning of the first great war, in 1914; with prescience, he felt that that first great war was coming, and kept the British Navy at sea so that it might be ready, its guns manned for action. This is the same Mr. Winston Churchill who was First Lord of the Admiralty back in 1911, 1912 and 1913, at a time when the then Prime Minister of Canada, Sir Robert Borden, wanted to do something to show the duty of this country to Great Britain and other parts of the empire.
Away back in those years Sir Robert Borden conferred with Mr. Winston Churchill, and the policy was then laid down whereby three dreadnoughts were to be built, the finest that science could devise or money could buy, It was Sir Robert Borden who in those years also laid down the policy that cruisers or destroyers would be built in Canada-a policy practically the same as that announced a few days ago in this chamber by the minister.
This statement was made either by Sir Robert Borden or by the present Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. Either of them could have said it:
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people wish indefinitely to continue a policy which demands of Great Britain the sole responsibility of guarding our trade routes, or which on the other hand takes shelter behind the existence on this continent of a great and friendly power. I believe that Canadian pride, Canadian dignity, Canadian

War Budget-Mr. Stirling
consciousness of present greatness, Canadian hope for increased stature among the nations of the world all demand that we should assume our proper share of the burden of naval service hitherto borne so largely by the motherland.
Those were not the words of Sir Robert Borden; they were the words of the present Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. He was born thirty years too late, or he would have been standing side by side and shoulder to shoulder with Sir Robert Borden thirty years ago. Had that policy been carried out then, had we been united within the empire in Canada, in south Africa and in Ireland, there are many people who believe that that first great war would not have taken place-and perhaps we would not have the present one.
The minister announced in the house that the government was going to establish a naval college as well as build destroyers in Canada.
I am sure those statements would not have been made by the minister unless they were to be carried out. I am sure that so far as the minister and the government are concerned, they have no political considerations with regard to matters of this kind. It is my view that the naval college should be located on the Atlantic coast. It was there in 1917, but was destroyed at that time by the great Halifax explosion. It should not be placed adjacent to balmy waters, but should be placed facing the north Atlantic, and in association with the fishermen of Nova Scotia, the Magdalen islands and of Newfoundland. Those men go down to the sea in ships, as the minister has described. There should be close contact with the British navy, with the stormy waters of the Atlantic and with the British people, and an understanding and friendly hand extended to the United States who are so anxious to cooperate with us with regard to naval matters.
I must hurry along to the discussion of a few more subjects with which I should like to deal. The largest industry in Nova Scotia is that of farming, but the farmers of that province are not prosperous. They receive low prices, and are faced with increasing costs. They have to compete with mass production, and the difficulties of processing and selling. They have made one request through their minister of agriculture in the local legislature, the Hon. John A. McDonald, and through their agricultural societies. That request is that they receive mill feeds at reduced freight rates, so that they might be placed on the same basis as were the people in Europe to whom those feeds were formerly exported.
The granaries of the west are overflowing. Our friends from the prairie provinces are anxious to dispose of their product, while the farmer of the maritime provinces wants those
products. The minister and other representatives have asked for that reduction in freight rates, but up to the present they have not been able to secure it. The result is that they are unable to obtain these feeds at prices which would permit them to make the necessary purchases to feed their stock.
The farmers of Nova Scotia wish to be placed upon the same basis as the farmers of the west as regards the control of water. Millions of dollars have been spent in the west to control water, but in the constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings, represented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), there are dyke lands that have gone out to sea. In my county of Cumberland and in Westmorland there are large acreages of land which attracted the early settlers, but which are covered by the sea or have reverted to floating bogs. This matter should receive attention from the government, and I should think this was as good a time as any to put some of the idle machinery in the Department of Public Works to use.

Mr. Speaker, I shall detain the house for but a few minutes because I desire to deal with just one phase of this motion. The measures which will result from the passing of these resolutions are for the purpose of enabling the government to conserve that comparatively small amount of United States exchange which is in our hands, for the purpose of buying from that country ever increasing quantities of materials, munitions and commodities of that sort required for the war. I am in full agreement with the desire which the government has in mind, and I referred to it when I spoke on the address ten days ago. My reason for being so strongly in
War Budget-Mr. Stirling

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my address on this resolution will by no means be the best during this debate, but I do lay claim to this one thing, that it will be the shortest.
This nation is at war. The budget resolutions are aimed at increasing our war effort. Upon their general principles I find myself

War Budget-Mr. Graydon

almost entirely in agreement with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), because it is of prime importance to Canada that our foreign exchange position be guarded and maintained.
My plea, however, is that the resolutions do not go quite far enough. I am not convinced that the government gave sufficiently careful or sympathetic consideration to the admittedly heavy Canadian purchases of fresh fruits and vegetables from the United States. In that I am in agreement with the previous speaker (Mr. Stirling), who gave in much more detail than I shall do the entire picture of this trade.
This importation is steadily on the rise and is seriously sapping the vitals of our foreign exchange status. This year we shall import approximately $23,000,000 worth of these commodities. Over half of these purchases are of a class or kind produced by our own growers who are in turn asked to assist our national war effort. Added also to that is the fact that, roughly speaking, we are using up almost $43,000,000 worth of precious exchange when we add the freight charges of something like $20,000,000 to the amount which I already gave; and this, Mr. Speaker, at a time when we need every cent of foreign exchange on which we can lay our hands in order to purchase engines of war from our neighbours.
I plead with the Minister of Finance tonight to give comprehensive, earnest and sympathetic consideration to what, I think, is a simple and direct governmental duty at this time.
Canada surely cannot be serious in thinking that the use of our money supplies to buy United States fresh fruits and vegetables can be an effective means of helping our war effort while similar products to those which we purchase lie rotting in our fields.
The question is simply this, and with it I conclude. Shall it be, for this country, fresh fruits and vegetables, or shall it be munitions and supplies from the United States? That, I think, is a simple question. As a matter of fact we cannot have both from the same Canadian dollar. I think I know the answer. I think the government knows the answer. I think the house knows the answer. And I am sure the people of the Dominion of Canada know the answer, too. Need I say more? Surely this is a time for action rather than for words.

I want to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) for his budget, but it does not go far enough. There may be a reason for not including all fruits and vegetables in schedule 1, which is the prohibitory schedule; but surely such fruits and vegetables as strawberries,
[Mr. Graydon.l
grapes and other small fruits, vegetables coming from Louisiana, Florida and California, and especially new potatoes and all grades of potatoes, should be prohibited, in view of the fact that we have in eastern Canada almost the largest surplus crop of potatoes in history, selling at half the cost of production, at a price of 20 cents a bushel to the grower. There are coming into Canada at the present time potatoes of a lower grade than the growers of Canada are allowed to ship to market. There is in the United States and Canada one of the largest crops of potatoes that we have had in a great many years, and the only shortage is in the provinces of Manitoba and Ontario. I contend that foreign exchange should not be allowed to be used for imported potatoes when we have a surplus crop in this country and the potato growers are able to supply our markets the year round.
According to the last Canada-United States trade agreement we are not allowed to ship potatoes to the United States except under a quota, but there is no quota or any other restriction upon United States potatoes entering Canada. Surely their potatoes, the production of which is assisted in every way by the United States department of agriculture, should not be allowed to come into Canada and compete with our Canadian potatoes at this time when our growers are selling their potatoes at less than half the cost of production, for that is what they are doing this season. These factories will not begin to handle the surplus of potatoes. Not only potato starch, but potato dextrine and wheat starch are needed in Great Britain. We are sending thousands of dollars out of Canada for the importation of com to be manufactured into corn starch in this country. This corn comes from south America and south Africa. Low grade wheat would make wheat starch which is equal to or better than corn starch, and also dextrine and a better grade of glucose than can be derived from corn. We are, however, sending away thousands of dollars for corn which comes in free of duty to be manufactured into corn starch. I suggest to the government that they get in touch with our corn-starch manufacturers and invite them to erect factories for the purposes I have mentioned. I believe the Canada Starch company have a factory at Fort William which they have not used for years and they could use the surplus of low grade wheat.
We cannot continue increasing the crop of potatoes in eastern Canada and the crop of wheat in the west for food purposes because we have at the present time more foodstuffs than the markets will absorb. Agriculture has come to the manufacturing stage and the sooner the government assists in the manufacturing of agricultural products, the better. Canada is the only country in the world to-day that is not assisting in this direction. The United States government has just voted $6,000,000 for the erection of four laboratories in that country to look into the

manufacture of power alcohol. Power alcohol will account for 80,000,000 bushels of western wheat, and low grade wheat at that.
We cannot go on in the west piling np wheat and building more storage space. Every bushel of wheat that goes into storage overhangs the market and every bushel that goes into a manufacturing plant is taken off the market. Wheat will make the finest starch, dextrine and glucose, and calls are coming now from the British empire, China, south Africa and south America, and all countries that are not blockaded. The textile trade of Great Britain is in need of starch, both potato and wheat dextrine.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put on the record a brief prepared by a chemical engineer who left Poland before the Germans entered. He had a plant for the manufacture of power alcohol from wheat, barley and soya beans. It was worth a million and a half dollars and he destroyed it before he left. Arguments for the Erection of Industrial Plants in Canada for the Production of Power Alcohol
A.	Present situation of the alcohol industry in Canada.
In 1938, alcohol production was about ten million proof gallons, including _ 4,250,000 gallons commercial alcohol. For this production, the following raw materials were imported:

Canada, having an overproduction of agricultural products suitable for the production of aloohol, imported over $2,000,000 of raw materials for this industry. By the new methods for producing alcohol from domestic raw	materials-potatoes	or grains:-it is
possible to obtain alcohol cheaper than1 from imported molasses and corn, and also by this-method to obtain very valuable residues (slops) rich in protein vitamins and yeast. These-residues are very valuable foodstuffs for cattle and poultry. From the production of ten million proof gallons annually, an amount of about 10,000 tons of this high value feed would be available.
Thus it is possible to liquidate the import of molasses and com for cattle food. The total amount of these imported products for industrial purposes and for cattle feeding amounted to the following for the year 1938:
Molasses ....gals. 12,600,000 value $ 2,180,000 Com	bus. 15,500,000	"	10,330,000
War Budget-Mr. Hatfield

B.	Importance of creating a power alcohol industry in Canada.
1.	Trade balance.
Canada imports $60,000,000 of petroleum products per year, and over $2,000,000 of tetra ethyl lead. The amount of these imports will increase on account of the development of motorization, and with the difference of exchange between the Canadian and American dollars.
The consumption of gasoline in Canada amounts to over 800,000,000 gallons per year. A blend of 20 per cent of alcohol (160,000,000 gallons) mixed with gasoline will not only improve the quality of gasoline from 63 to 80 octanes, but will save in trade balance about $15,000,000 per year in imported petroleum products.
When producing 100,000,000 gallons of absolute alcohol per year from grains and potatoes, Canada will get about 320,000 tons of the above mentioned valuable foodstuffs. This cheap fodder will increase the production of milk and eggs; will create conditions for the breeding of cattle and pigs, and will also be the basis of a new industry of next products, thus liquidating the import of animals and animal products, which amount at present to .$30,000,000 per year.
2.	Profits for Agriculture.
Canada produces per year the following average amount of grains and potatoes:-
Wheat	
bushels	300,000,000Oats	
bushels	330,000,000Barley	
bushels	80,000,000Rye	
bushels	10,000,000Potatoes	cwts.	40,000,000
The value of field crops amounts to $600,000,000 per year. Because of the overproduction, and lack of export in some years, this figure decreases to less than $500,000,000. This difference is a big loss for the farmers.
When adding 20 per cent of alcohol to gasoline, we create a consumption of 160,000,000 gallons of power alcohol per year. This quantity of alcohol would need 80,000,000 bushels of grain, and would provide every year a "safety valve" in the grain price market, by taking this amount of grain out of the market for good. From the economic point of view, the production of power alcohol is not less important than the grain elevators problem was some years ago. Grain elevators provide for the storing of grain only. Modern alcohol factories, using agricultural products, decidedly rid the markets of agricultural overproduction, which does not return to the markets at a later date. Moreover, the cost of investment in a modern alcohol factory for one ton of processed grain is not greater than the construction cost of the same amount of grain elevators. Producing alcohol from grain saves the cost of grain storage. Alcohol is usually produced from the lower grades of grain, which increased therefore the value of the other grades of grain. Constructing an alcohol factory where the grain grows, saves 70 per cent of its weight in the cost of transport, or 90 per cent when dealing with potatoes. The weight of the alcohol produced from grain amounts to 30 per cent of the weight of the grain, or 10 per cent of the weight of potatoes. Besides this, the farmer gets the valuable fodder mentioned above, which gives him the possibility of an additional revenue on the breeding of cattle and poultry,

receiving at no charge a great amount of fertilizer. Thus he reduces the cost of the production of grain.
3.	Indirect profits of development of the
power alcohol industry for the economic life in Canada.
The construction cost of a modern factory to produce 10,000 gallons of alcohol daily is estimated at $500,000. If the industry were to be developed to the extent mentioned, i.e.,
160,000,000 gallons annually, a capital investment of $25,000,000 would be necessary. The buildings and machinery equipment can be executed in this country. Thus the building and machinery industries would be able to give work to a large number of unemployed. The new alcohol industry itself would be able to give permanent work to 5,000 workers, not including the farmers nor the industries connected with the alcohol production.
The fifteen years' experience of 35 countries of the world which introduced the production of power alcohol, indicates that these countries not only did not suffer though cancelling the taxes of the power alcohol which takes the place of taxed gasoline, but received them back from the improved agriculture, through the decrease of money grants to farmers and unemployed, also saving at the same time many foreign payments already mentioned. During the last few years, Brazil, Italy, and Japan, increased many times the power alcohol production. Now, Australia is developing a great programme of production.
Among the agricultural countries, Canada is the only one which has not done anything yet about this important industry.
4.	The alcohol industry and the war.
The war is a great consumer of alcohol, as it is required for the production of explosives, and other war needs. Production of alcohol in England is based on imported molasses. Because of transport difficulties, it would seem useful to construct immediately some alcohol plants in Canada, using domestic raw materials. Canada, being free from air raids and invasion would be able to deliver alcohol to England in connection with its war programme of supplies.
C.	Execution of the programme.
The construction of a power alcohol plant under actual conditions, would require at least eight months. Considering the large area of Canada, it would be wise to construct two or three plants at once, in different centres of large agricultural overproduction. These pilot factories would give practical results as to the cost of production, as well as the economic point of view. The results obtained would give a basis for the construction of other factories.
D.	Recapitulation.
The creation of power alcohol production in Canada would give the following benefits:
1.	Decrease imports per year as follows:
Molasses and corn	 $12,000,000
Petroleum products	 15,000,000
Animals and animal products 30,000,000
2.	Protect agriculture against marketing losses of $50,000,000 to $100,000,000 per year.
3.	Increase taxable revenues from the more profitable agriculture and the new industry in alcohol.
4.	Reduce unemployment in agriculture and industry.
5.	Save cost of transporting 70 per cent of
80,000,000 bushels of grain annually.

War Budget-Mr. Hatfield
6.	Save cost of storing 80,000,000 bushels of grain annually.
7.	Supply agriculture with a cheap valuable fodder as well as fertilizer, and create the basis of increased animal production and meat industry.
8.	Ensure delivery of a great amount of alcohol for war purposes from domestic raw materials.
9.	The use of the lower grades of grain in such large quantities will increase considerably the value of the rest of the grain.
10.	Provide a "safety valve" for the grain price market, even of more importance and utility than the grain elevators question a few years ago.
(The basic figures given in above report can be confirmed by the Canada Year Book, 1939.)
I should like to see the Department of Agriculture do something to assist the potato growers of eastern Canada especially in the maritimes. We have no market in the United States this year. Our export market has been shut off.
I wish to commend the Minister of Trade and Commerce for his trade mission to south America. I believe I brought this matter up in June. It is late, but better late than never. I suggest, however, that they will have to go further than a trade mission. The United States government has been building a steamer a month for the last ten months and turning these ships over to the operators for the purpose of capturing the trade which Germany and the Scandinavian countries had in south America before the war. We need shipping facilities to south America. There is a very large trade there for the agricultural products of Canada.
The bacon agreement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) while in the old country is lower by $2.28 a hundred than the former agreement, and in the meantime prices of mill feeds and of everything else that go into the production of hogs have risen, so that our eastern farmers are up against it and are cutting out the raising of hogs.
I see that the war-time prices and trade board has fixed a maximum price for butter. Why should it fix a maximum price for butter when it has fixed a minimum on apples and wheat? If we want the dairymen of Canada to take their milk to the cheese factories there is no need to use force. The dairymen are loyal and they will cooperate. All the government has to do is to tell them that cheese is required instead of butter. There is no need to fix a maximum price for butter. It can go as low as you like, but it cannot go higher, and if butter is in the hands of speculators it should not be. The government should have some system of handling butter in surplus periods in the summer months, and the farmer who makes the butter should have the benefit of the excess price in the winter.
May I say something now about fertilizer and fertilizer chemicals. When the war import tax of 10 per cent was imposed it covered fertilizer. Our fertilizer chemicals have to be imported. The exchange tax of 10 per cent meant to our farmers, who are selling their produce below cost of production, an advance of from $3 to $4 a ton. Only one fertilizer chemical is produced here, namely, sulphate of ammonia. That is handled by one firm who immediately advanced the price $4 a ton or 10 per cent. This should not be allowed.
There is no reason why we should send out foreign exchange for the importation of corn. I would suggest that the government establish a committee to look into the question. The Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce should study the whole subject. We should be using up our low grade western wheat. Two hundred million bushels of wheat could be used in the manufacture of starch dextrine, glucose and power alcohol. Two million dollars' worth of tetra ethyl lead is imported, raising the octane value of gasoline. Power alcohol, wheat alcohol or potato alcohol would give the same results.
I suggest that the government do away with the central experimental farm and turn over the experiments to the national research council. The council is doing a wonderful job in Ottawa, whereas the farm has outlived its usefulness. There are enough offices at the central experimental farm without building more. Agriculture to-day is not bothered with the problem of production. It has surpluses. Give the farmer a decent return for his products and he will soon find ways of producing them. It is not the production we need so much as the marketing.
The people of Canada are tired of the waste that is going on in our war effort. They are tired of seeing money spent for the construction of small arms factories and so on. Nothing but aeroplanes will win this war, and an aeroplane factory should be built in every province.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words *on the motion and the amendment. First, I should like to endorse the statements made yesterday by the acting leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell); that is, the budget proposals in the main are satisfactory, as far as they go. Measures will have to be taken to ensure that prices of home products are not increased where importations are restricted or prohibited. The necessary safeguards, however, I think can be better discussed when we are dealing with the items in the schedules. My purpose in rising at this time is to support the amendment proposed yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and seconded by myself. Our amendment has two virtues: it is very simple, and it is very direct. I should like to read it again for the benefit of hon. members. It reads:
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that the government has not seen fit to introduce proposals for the raising of a compulsory war loan free of interest to be levied according to ability to subscribe."
In his two speeches on the address in reply to the speech from the throne the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) referred at considerable length to the last war loan. Speaking just last Tuesday, he referred to the failure of the loan and the necessity of finding some procedure to get large numbers of individual investors to subscribe. He said that he did not know what the cure was, but that there would have to be concerted action. Well, we are proposing concerted action, and, moreover, action that is in conformity with the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act of 1940. I will quote the important section of that act, which reads:
2. Subject to the provisions of section three hereof, the governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things, and make from time to time such orders and regulations, requiring persons to place themselves, their services and their property at the disposal of his majesty in the right of Canada, as may be deemed necessary or expedient for securing the public safety, the defence of Canada, the maintenance of public order, or the efficient prosecution of the war, or for maintaining supplies or services essential to the life of the community.
{Mr. Hatfield.]
When the amendment was proposed yesterday, I thought I detected hostility to it from the attitude of certain hon. members opposite. I am at a loss to understand why that should be the situation, since these members gave their unanimous support to the National Resources Mobilization Act less than six months ago. The ipurpose of that act, as is clear from the section I read, was to give the government power to take whatever measures were necessary for the effective mobilization of the resources of this country, both human and material, for the prosecution of the war. At the time that act was under discussion this group pointed out that we were fearful, because of past experience, that in its operation the act would be applied only to persons and not to property. So far the act has been applied only to persons. In reply to our expressed fears in that regard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said, according to Hansard for June 18, 1940, at page 902:
The measure is intended to cover every resource that the country has, human and material. But may I ask my hon. friends this question:	What justification is there for
assuming that it is only going to be the provisions of the measure related to the human that will be invoked and not the material? Is not any fair-minded man entitled to say that there is just as much reason to assume that this bill is introduced solely for the purpose of applying it to material things?
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said:
Experience of the past.
Then the Prime Minister went on:
Not experience of the past. I absolutely deny that statement. Does my hon. friend mean to say to me he believes I place more value in material things than I do on human life?
The fact of the matter is that we were at that time fearful that this act would apply only to human beings, and we stressed that point. We tried in every possible way to get this house to put itself on record that it would deal with material things first. What has transpired since the act was passed last June is sufficient proof that we were wise in taking heed of our past experience.
The young men who have been called up since the national registration are wondering why the act should apply to them, why they should be registered, tabulated and on call. They know that if they do not show up at the appointed place at the appointed time, a policeman will knock at their doors and find out very quickly the reason why. They wonder why all this is done, when no attempt is being made to take the wealth of people who have been bleeding this country since and even during the last war.

War Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
In my home city of Vancouver young men in their 'teen age are walking the streets without anything to do, and without a place to lay their heads. They are sleeping in boxcars and empty buildings-any place they can find. As soon as they reach the age of twenty-one they will have to answer the call and take their turn at training, in order that they may give their lives, if necessary, to defend a country which will not feed them.
I think it is far more appropriate that people to whom the country has been kind, people who have been able to amass large amounts of this world's wealth, and who have been able to lay that money to one side, should be called upon at this time of need to give of their means and their wealth in defence of their country, without waiting until it in its extremity will have to give them higher interest rates or higher wages for their money.
Why should there be any opposition to compulsion? As I have said, we have already voted for compulsion. This house has approved it; it is on the statute books; it is the law; it is being applied to human beings. Then, why should there be any opposition to its application to money or to wealth? Surely, when hon. members voted for the National Resources Mobilization Act, they did not make mental reservations. Surely they did not from their experience of the past conclude that it would not apply or that it would not be used to take property. But let us consider this matter of compulsion. Is not all taxation a matter of compulsion? So far as compulsion is concerned, what is the difference between digging into the pay envelope of the young man or young girl, old man or old girl, if you like, who gets a measly $50 or $60 a month, and taking out 2 per cent of the wage and calling it a national defence tax,

Yet we take 2 per cent out of the pay envelopes of those girls mentioned the other evening by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), whose wages are so little that the only breakfast they can afford is a cup
and taking from the savings of those who have been receiving anywhere from $5,0Q0 to $50,000 or more a year for the past number of years, and asking them to lend a part of it without interest to the country in its time of emergency?
There is no ethical difference in the world, so far as the two cases I have mentioned are concerned. If there is any difference, and if any different method should be applied, surely it is the person who is getting the low wage who should be exempt, and not the other person who has a good living and idle money.
I believe I read somewhere in a bankers' magazine that the real purpose of savings certificates and of urging persons of small means to subscribe to war loans is not so much to get the money but rather to take the money out of circulation, so that it will not be used for ordinary consumption purposes. subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON PROPOSALS OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR CONSERVATION OF FOREIGN EXCHANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the war budget now under consideration by the house is closely related to the financial and economic position of the country. That is why I have decided to make a few brief remarks in what I believe to be the interests of the Canadian people.
As regards the amendment presented by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold well), it would seem to be but another attempt at conscripting wealth. We must therefore reject it as should be rejected conscription of any nature, for in the preparation of a budget, as in all things, our first care must be to avoid imperilling the economic life of the nation.
Agriculture is, particularly in war time, our principal industry. To lessen agricultural production, to take away the labour essential to its prosperity would be a tragic mistake. The various countries vanquished by Germany were subdued through lack of food and munitions. In these difficult times, agriculture must not only carry on but develop and expand. Farm production, intensified and reorganized with the assistance of public bodies, will triumph over the obstacles that lie in the path of sacrifice whereon treads a world in distress. Liberty, justice and right cannot successfully oppose barbarism without the support of that living force that is agriculture.
Many have suggested that the training period of our young men be extended from one to four months. Such a measure would be most inopportune. It would paralyse agricultural production and consequently this country's war effort. Numerous are the young farmers, journeymen and technicians who have had to request from their local registrars delays and postponement of their training under the mobilization act. Such postpone-

ments are granted however only in extremely serious or special cases. It has been said that the training of young farmers at the end of autumn and during the winter would not impair agricultural production. This is not correct. A great many young men and as many heads of families have pointed out to me that it would be impossible for them to find the help required for the maintenance of production figures and the sound management of their farms. Certain farmers in my riding sell a great deal of milk the whole year round. Many of them are the owners of certified herds, having invested in the dairy industry the greater part of their assets. Concerned with public hygiene, they have erected their farm buildings according to plans and specifications furnished by the governments. Briefly, there exists for them no off season, no more than for any progressive farmer to my knowledge.
The same remarks apply in the case of market gardeners. There are in my riding a great many hot-house owners who produce fresh vegetables all winter long. Their installation and equipment costs have been rather high. Why should we now add to their already heavy burden of poor returns for farm produce that of a scarcity of labour. Therefore do I demand for agriculture and all the vital industries of the nation, on which depend the economic balance and the salvation of this country, all the assistance required not only to pass through a trying period but also for the solution of those distressing post-war problems. When the present conflict has reached an end, the lost peoples of the earth will turn to the land in their supreme struggle for life. What industry better than agriculture will then be able to resist the far-reaching reactions provoked by war? In so far as it is essential to life, thus will its decline paralyse all initiative. Side by side with armament plants erected at the cost of enormous sacrifices, the governments should build a first rate agricultural industry.
The worst enemies of agriculture are: the desertion of rural areas, war profiteering and the unfair distribution of taxes. Sixty years ago or more, the farm population of Quebec represented four-fifths of the total population in that province. The exodus toward the cities, begun in the years following 1880, has been increasing ever since and to such an extent that there exists to-day a terrifying lack of balance in this regard. At the moment, two-thirds of the population of Quebec live in urban centres. In the face of such a deplorable economic situation, what policy should our governments follow? They should endeavour to prevent this wholesale desertion of our rural districts by adopting measures destined to en-

War Budget-Mr. Ilsley
courage and protect agriculture; to promote understanding and appreciation of agriculture through education, farmers' organizations and cooperation; to check by every means profiteers who exploit the poverty and efforts of the producer and the consumer.
While there were more than fifty million pounds of butter stored in various warehouses throughout the country, we recently experienced a rise in the price of this commodity to the sole profit of the speculator. The price obtained by the producer for his milk remained in fact the same, and both he and the consumer were thus exploited. One might make the same observation in connection with a great many other farm products. How can such reprehensible speculative operations be tolerated at a moment when the workmen of the soil and the factory are making enormous sacrifices? Taxes of all kinds have been placed not only upon luxuries but also upon the necessaries of life. Consider, for instance, the tax placed upon containers destined to our home industries, and the additional taxes upon the very products of such industries. Let us beware of awakening one day to find agriculture in an irreparably exhausted state. Let us keep on the land the labour essential to its development. Let us not tear away from agriculture the youth in whom rests the survival of this nation. Nowhere else could they render greater service to their country than on the farm. The day agriculture is sacrificed, then may we expect the worst to befall us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few words to say on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The habit has grown in this debate of referring to the speech that I made here last Monday as a budget, and to the proposals as budget proposals. I think it is unfortunate that members should have fallen into the habit of referring to it in that way because it has led us into many speeches some of which I think perhaps would not have been made had the purpose of these proposals been kept more clearly in mind. The budget, of course, is a different thing entirely. The budget estimates the revenues and expenditures for the coming year and ordinarily proposes the imposition of taxes, presents a financial statement, and otherwise deals with the financial affairs of the 1 country. But this was in no sense a budget. These proposals have one purpose and one purpose alone, namely, the conservation of foreign exchange. Such taxation measures as were proposed were incidental and supplementary to the main proposals which were for the object I have mentioned. I was very careful in the proposals to leave 14873-46
out anything of a taxation nature or anything which could be construed as being introduced for the purpose of raising revenue.
There are measures which I should have liked to introduce in the house this session if the circumstances had been just a little different. For instance, I announced in September last that income taxpayers would have the privilege of paying their income tax by instalments; that is, the income tax which will be due on April 30 next. If the taxpayer should pay one-third of his tax in four monthly instalments before April 30, he would have the privilege of paying the other two-thirds of his income tax in four equal monthly instalments following April 30. It is necessary that this be authorized by act of parliament, and I was tempted to include that proposal among the proposals submitted at this session, but I purposely left it out because I did not want the house to fall into any confusion about the purpose of these particular proposals. They are introduced for one purpose and for one purpose alone.
The procedure was to move that the Speaker do leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means. I believe that under the standing orders it is possible under a motion of that kind to move an amendment such as the one proposed. But while that may be, I presume, technically possible under the rules, nevertheless it is not, I submit, a proper amendment for consideration on its merits by the house at the present time. It is simply a motion of non-confidence in the government and must be regarded by the government as such. It is equivalent to saying this: The government is moving that the Speaker do leave the chair for the house to consider certain proposals for the conservation of exchange, but I, the mover of the amendment, and my supporters, think that, instead of doing that, the house should go on record as condemning the government for having taken the wrong line in its general financial policy. Of course that is a serious motion, and if it were to be treated on the merits it would require a full discussion, a great deal of debate, and so forth. But I do not think the house or the country will expect us at this stage, before the Christmas recess, to depart from the consideration of exchange conservation measures into a broad discussion of general financial policy. I hope not, and I think that is the feeling of the house and also the feeling of the people whose eyes are upon us here.
So, Mr. Speaker, I am going to content myself to-night with simply pointing out

War Budget-Division

to the house that, if the amendment passes, we are prevented from considering the exchange conservation measures because the Speaker will not leave the chair. Those words, if the amendment carried, would be struck out, and we would be prevented frbm considering exchange conservation measures which I believe everybody in the house agrees are necessary and urgently necessary.
I would also point out that, if the amendment carries, it is equivalent to a vote of non-confidence in the administration and would be followed of course by the results which normally attend such a vote. I would suggest, therefore, that the house deal with the amendment on those considerations. At the proper time there is no objection at all to amendments or proposals of this kind being considered on their merits, and we will consider them on their merits. But I am suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that this is not the time and the place, and I am going to ask the house to reject the amendment, for these reasons.

The importation of automobiles into Canada will be prohibited under the provisions of the War Exchange Conservation Act, when it is passed, and it is not desired simply to transfer the business from those selling imported automobiles to those selling domestic automobiles.

That the importation into Canada of any goods enumerated and described in schedule one is prohibited except in such cases as the Minister of National Revenue in his discretion deems desirable and under and in accordance with the terms of a permit granted by him: Provided however that this prohibition shall not apply to-
(a)	any goods imported from, and being of the growth, produce or manufacture of, any country within the sterling area or Newfoundland, except, at the discretion of the Minister of National Revenue, goods composed wholly or in part of silk;
(b)	any goods which on or before the second day of December, 1940, were in .transit to Canada.

I should
like to make a few observations with respect to this matter. I made reference to it yesterday. Is there not some other method by which these exceptions could be handled? This measure provides that with regard to goods intended to be prohibited under this measure there may be exceptions in the discretion of the Minister of National Revenue, under the terms of a permit to be granted by him. This seems to me to be the wrong way to handle this matter. What would be the considerations that would actuate the minister in exercising his discretion and issuing a permit? What standards, what principles would he rely upon? Would every case be judged upon its own merits, or is there to be set up some standard which would guide the minister? I do not for a moment suggest that the present minister would abuse the exercise of his discretion,

but this discretion is capable of great abuse, and it is bad legislation because of that fact. Certainly I abject to the principle and spirit of this type of legislation. I dare say we have gone a long way beyond this in the delegation of power, but as far as I am concerned I am going to register an objection to the principle involved. I think we ought to deal with the matter in another way. Either we are going to keep out these goods, or we are not.
This prohibition does not apply to goods in transit, of course, so no question arises there. If we are going to keep out imports for the purpose the minister intends, that of conserving our foreign exchange, there should not be any loophole which would enable any friend of the government to come and say, "I must have this thing here." The minister might accede to the demand, while some man not so important, who would not be able to pull as many strings, may I say, would be denied the same right. That sort of thing does happen under party government; make no mistake about it. This is not exactly a war measure. It is a measure designed to aid the war effort, but it leaves too much power in the hands of the minister.-any minister-and I object to the delegation of power to any minister which will give him authority to say that John Jones may have this article brought in while Tom Brown may not have it. That is wrong, and I believe the matter can be handled in some other way.
If the minister is really desirous of keeping out certain articles let him go the whole length. I assume that this will not apply to goods ordered legitimately and1 now in process of transit or even of manufacture. I would help out a man who had entered into a contract even though the goods were not actually in transit. But to say that the minister shall be entitled, on representations made to him, to give a permit to somebody to bring in something that it is intended by parliament shall be kept out for the duration of the war, while somebody else cannot obtain a permit, I submit is all wrong. If I argued the thing for an hour I could not put it any more concretely than that.

As a matter of fact, this whole thing could have been done by order in council, but we placed it before parliament because it is a matter of great importance and something upon which parliament should pass. But in time of war abundant powers are vested in the executive to do almost anything by order in council, and the government has to decide what steps must be taken from day to day. Parliament is not in session all the time, and it is necessary to do these things.
Certainly it is not the intention of the government to make any changes in principle, or any sweeping changes or anything like that, by order in council, but that may have to be done. I debated with myself whether I should put in this measure a provision giving power to the governor in council to amend this list, to add to or take away from it. I did not think I would do that, because already the government has that power under the War Measures Act, and I think perhaps they also have power in certain cases under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. I thought I ought to tell the committee and the house that in working this matter out it may be necessary as time goes on to make changes by order in council. I say that because when we meet again I do not want anybody to say, "Oh, well, after parliament got away there was an order in council put through altering one or two of these items."
That might have to be done, but of course that is a different matter from the point raised by the hon. gentleman. He is talking about the discretion vested in the Minister of National Revenue. And that is the way it ought to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, if we can think of everything.

I suggested that idea to the minister. It does not apply to goods in transit, and I suggested it should not apply to goods under contract which were not in transit. If that is the intention in this instance, then say so in the statute. The minister should say so in the resolution, just as he has with respect to goods in transit.
My point goes far beyond that. It comes to this, that there should not be vested in the minister power to issue a permit to an importer in respect of any one of these classes of goods which it is intended, in the general principle, shall be kept out. If we are proceeding on a proper principle, then six months hence no power should be given to bring goods in.
Then, with respect to the cases to which the minister has referred, I would say that that would simply be a matter of justice, and ought to be in the statutes. It could be easily placed there. In fact, I do not know why the draftsman did not put those in when he was putting in goods in transit. He could, by

War Exchange Conservation Act
appropriate and apt expressions, provide for goods under contract, such as those to which the minister has referred, and to which I refer. That is the way it ought to be.
I object to the principle involved in this part of the resolution. I do not wish, however, to take time to argue it, because I am trying to get through. If I argued it all night I could not make it more emphatic than I have.

I believe this is the first time that the principle of giving a minister of the crown such discretion has ever been asked. It amounts to an abnegation of the right of parliament, as I see it. Already the governor in council has very wide powers under the War Measures Act. The minister says that the governor in council has the power to do that which is now being delegated to the minister. If this particular section is to cover only part I of schedule 1, I submit it should be so stated. The minister has said it is his intention and that of the government that the interpretation to be placed on this resolution is to make it applicable only to part I.
The minister will realize that the intention of the government will not be taken into consideration in the interpretation of the statute. I would suggest that at least in the first place part I be added to schedule 1, if the government insists upon passing the resolution as it now stands.
Second, I take objection to the wording.
It says:
That the importation into Canada of any goods enumerated and described in schedule one is prohibited except in such cases as the Minister of National Revenue in his discretion deems desirable-
And so on. I do not understand the use of the words "in such cases." Does that mean that the minister may say to one individual, "You may import certain goods," and to another individual, "You shall remain subject to the prohibitions in schedule 1." I do not think that can be the meaning of it.
If the meaning is that it refers to goods, and not to individuals, then I suggest that the words "in such cases" should be altered to read "for such goods." Generally speaking, I submit that this is one of the most flagrant delegations of power on the part of parliament to an individual minister that has been asked by this government. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that having the powers already, under the War Measures Act, to do that which he now wishes conferred upon the Minister of National Revenue, is sufficient. This is too great a delegation of power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The changing of the phrase "in such cases" to "for such goods" is perfectly
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.j
all right, so far as part I is concerned, if the committee wishes so to do. It will be understood, of course, that no matter what the committee does or no matter how it is phrased, powers exist under the War Measures Act to go beyond or to repeal and go all round the statute. It is all very well for us to take great pains with the drafting, but those powers exist. They are not taken away.
So it comes to a question of trusting the governor in council but not trusting the minister. There may be a distinction there, but I do not think it is a valid one. I was going to say that the intention, so far as part I is concerned, is that all individuals will be treated exactly alike. That is, no individual in any particular period will be given a permit to import a certain class or kind of goods, and at the same time another individual be denied that permit. That will never be done under part I.
But under part II it may be necessary for that very thing to be done, depending upon the stock of goods, or the requirements of the person applying for the permit. Perhaps this could be torn to pieces in such a way as to tie it down a little more definitely as between these two parts of the act. Then, if it did not work in any particular we would have to alter it by order in council, under the War Measures Act.
Does the draft bill follow the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I believe so.
I can find no reference in the resolution to part II of schedule 1. Why is there not some reference? Why are there parts I and II; what is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I explained exactly what
we intended to do, and the different treatment we proposed to extend to goods under part II
as compared with those under part I. Those under part I are prohibited goods. Those under part II are goods which are not prohibited, but concerning which permits are to be diminished, as time goes on.
Tapered off.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Why is that not put in the resolution? Why is there no reference to part II in the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was just saying that if the committee wishes to have such reference, there would be no objection. It would really have no further control.

Will it be in the bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

There
ought to be some redrafting, then. The minister suggests that even though the matter is dealt with in a stricter fashion, and the language is tied right down along the lines suggested, it could be overruled under the War Measures Act. Remember, this is a later statute, and if it is specific there might be a very nice conflict between those two statutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

Oh, yes. Have the law officers of the crown given consideration to that situation? The War Measures Act is a general law. This is a specific law. Parliament is legislating on a specific matter, and if this law fastens the interpretation specifically, then I suggest to the minister that the courts, in a proper case, would look into the matter very carefully. The specific legislation would override the general legislation which was passed subsequently.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would mean that all acts passed since the War Measures Act was passed in 1914 would be limited in their application by that act, and the hands of the government tied accordingly.
It raises a very nice legal point, but I am not going to give an expert opinion.
What impelled the government to ask for these powers when the governor in council had them already under the War Measures Act? They are being extended and granted to a minister of the crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was done out of respect for parliament. It was well understood by the government that this could be done under the War Measures Act. When the debate on the address ended two or three days ago the house could have been adjourned and then, any time after, we had the power to act under the War Measures Act, because if ever there was a war measure, this is one. We did not think, however, that would be acting in the true spirit of the constitution of this country. We thought that when parliament was here we ought to lay the matter before parliament and state what we intended to do. We must have wide and inflexible powers. It was thought we should tell parliament that we intended to take the powers and then work it out. As I say, parliament can wrestle over these clauses and tie the minister down a little tighter or make it clear that it is only in respect of one thing that he has certain
powers and so on, but I do not think that is the thing to do as a practical matter. If we run into a situation which requires correction we may have to refer to the War Measures Act, and certainly we will refer to it in order to correct such a situation. If anyone finds that the government is being unjust, that it is treating a supporter differently from the manner in which it is treating someone who is not a supporter, then he will just have to bring the case to the attention of the government. That would be a disgraceful thing, and it will not happen.

I congratulate the minister upon having realized that it is time to get back to the authority and supremacy of parliament. We have gone too far in the other direction in Canada. I have been harping on this off and on for six months, and I am glad that we have made the government do this.
Do not make my speeches.

Can the minister give the committee a rough idea of the total importations in the last fiscal year and how they will be affected by the two parts of schedule I, and also let us know from which different countries these importations came?

It could be stated in the bill that it would terminate with the cessation of hostilities. In his speech the other day the minister referred to the possibility which we all must see of this prohibition of the entry of certain articles being likely to cause an increase in the price of similar articles produced in Canada. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have an amendment to move to this resolution, as follows:
That the resolution of December 2, 1940, introducing a measure to be called the War Exchange Conservation Act, 1940, be amended by striking out resolution No. 4 and substituting therefor the following:
"4. (1) That in the event of any person taking advantage of the prohibition of imports to increase the prices of goods to the consumer or to maintain the prices of such goods at levels deemed by the governor in council to be higher than should prevail, having regard to changes in the cost of production of such goods, the governor in council may, in addition to permitting entry of such goods, reduce or remove the duties of customs imposed upon such goods.
(2) That in the event of any person taking advantage of the prohibition of imports as aforesaid, the governor in council may, for such period of time ae he may determine, impose, levy and collect upon all the products of such person or any of them, an excise tax of 25 per cent of the sale price thereof payable by such person at the time of delivery of such goods to the purchaser thereof and the provisions of the Special War Revenue Act as to the collection of taxes imposed by Part XIII of the said act shall be applicable thereto."
The change is from "producers" to "any person". The resolution is being made all-inclusive, whereas before it was just confined to producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct. The reason for this amendment is that the original resolution was taken verbatim from section 17 of

War Exchange Conservation Act
the customs tariff. The amended wording should accomplish the purpose of this resolution rather more effectively.
The amendment will enable the government to proceed against any person, whereas section 17 applied only to producers of goods. It also provides for an excise tax of 25 per cent on the sale price of the goods, whereas under section 17 the tax is equivalent to the amount of customs duty which would be paid by such goods if imported into Canada under the general tariff.
These prohibitions relate to goods some of which are free. We just made a mistake there when we provided for imposing customs duty as a penalty.
This is the first time I remember hearing the minister admit making a mistake..

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I move the amendment, Mr. Chairman, that has been read by the Minister of Finance.

Before that is put, I raise again the point I raised yesterday. Instead of this procedure being followed, I think it would be better if the house enacted that the prices of goods shall remain at the prices in existence say on the 2nd day of December, and in the event of producers desiring an increase in prices on account of changed conditions they shall make application to the war-time prices and trade board, which will consider the application.
I do not think the method suggested by the government is sufficiently effective. I believe that we should stabilize prices as of, say the 2nd day of December, and then in the event of changed conditions an application may be made to the proper board for consideration of a proposed price increase. I think that suggestion should be considered. I believe it would be much more satisfactory to the public who already feel that some price increases have been permitted. It is difficult for the general public to appeal to a board, whereas a producer who felt he was penalized by changed conditions could easily make application and get consideration of his case. I want to place that point of view before the minister.

I would suggest to the minister that my hon. friend, I think, has not thought his suggestion clear through. If prices were pegged as of December 2, it might work a great hardship if costs of production were increased by abnormal conditions.

The producer could
apply to the board.
That is regimentation. A price increase might be justified by increased costs of production or by other factors. I think my hon. friend's suggestion would not be workable. I prefer the penalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On some occasion, I cannot remember when, because it was not in my department, I had a discussion with the wartime prices and trade board as to the two methods they might follow. One was to make a stand-still order on prices and to let everyone apply for an increase in prices. The objection to that was that the board would be swamped with applications. That plan would not be administratively possible. There are a great many prices in Canada and a great many people charging prices.
They are doing that in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know about that.
That, I understand, is their method.
There is a question of principle involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The civil service required
to attend to that effectively would be very extensive because the ramifications are tremendous. The board could not with any sense of responsibility be issuing permissions to increase prices unless they went into the matter carefully because every increase in price that persons could persuade the board to permit them to make would be justified by the authority of the board. The board would be cited as the reason why the price was increased. It was therefore considered much more desirable for the board to require everybody to report to them when they intended to increase prices or when they did increase prices, and for the board to get a reasonably large staff which, if they saw any price increase which prima facie appeared to be unwarranted or unreasonable, would investigate and require the person increasing the price to justify it. That was considered a much more practical way, and I think it is. I do not think there has been much complaint about it either. I believe it has worked well.

There is a
danger on the other hand that the public may get swamped. There are two provisions in resolution 4. First, if it is discovered that a man is taking advantage of this measure of protection, the prohibition will be removed. But if it is removed, the whole purpose of the legislation, which is to conserve exchange,

War Exchange Conservation Act
will be defeated. Therefore that rules the first out, because it would defeat the purpose of the measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only for that item.

Yes, but what if the same thing happens in connection with other items? The government's measure, will no longer be operative.
The second provision is that where a person has been found to be taking advantage of the prohibition of imports, the 25 per cent excise tax will be applied. But would a 25 per cent excise tax be sufficient to offset the advantage of an industry that is now given a complete monopoly by virtue of the fact that certain lines of goods from non-empire countries are completely shut out? The 25 per cent tax may not be a sufficient penalty to offset the protection they are going to enjoy. I do not think in either case the minister is giving us sufficient assurance that prices will be kept at a moderate figure and that advantage will not be taken of this virtual monopoly which is now going to be given to certain industries in Canada.
May I point out further that we do not know what machinery will be set up to decide whether or not an industry or a particular firm is taking advantage of the situation. Who will decide, for example, and inform the governor in council that a certain producer is taking advantage of the prohibition of imports? Will it be the Department of National Revenue or the war-time prices and trade board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government holds itself free to use any agency it wishes.
Or none at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend does not give other Canadians as much credit as he should. That is his trouble. I have listened to him a great many times. He feels that people who have a chance to make a lot of money are going to do it. He goes on that principle. But there are such things as public opinion and patriotism in this country, and such things as a sense of decency and a sense of responsibility on the part of the government of the country, and all these things work together at a time like this.
I have seen people under the pressure of public opinion here and there in connection with government activities, and they want to do the right thing. They want their fellow Canadians to feel that they are doing the right thing. They want to do it in their own interests, in the interests of their reputation, and in the interests of the way they and their families will be treated. There is not just

this one narrow idea of gouging the last cent out of people all the time. All these factors I have mentioned are going to work together.
In the national revenue department I found that 95 per cent of the sales taxpayers-the sales tax was the largest-were honest, and there was only about 5 per cent with whom we had any trouble. Most of these taxpayers were honest and decent. I do not anticipate that there is going to be any mad rush to put prices up to the limit behind the shelter of this prohibition. If there is, we shall hear about it; do not make any mistake. When a person sells goods, somebody buys the goods; it is well known when people begin profiteering, and we can get after them and in various ways take action to see that they bring their prices down. We have not, I admit, set up any machinery here, but we have left ourselves free to use any agency or all agencies. If there is any profiteering out of this, we shall hear of it and we shall do something about it.

The minister has certainly strengthened the resolution. Does he say that these provisions are adequate to maintain a decent standard of prices without profiteering? If the minister believes that, and the government intends to carry it on that way, I am quite satisfied. They must use any agency they can use; I agree with that statement.
Really we are only prohibiting the import of these goods from nonsterling countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Practically everything which is on the list can be imported from one or other of the empire countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A great many of them.

There is that competition. How can we fix the price when we do not know what the cost will be from empire countries? It is not a complete prohibition. It is only a prohibition from certain countries; that is all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true.

May I point out to the minister that he is not altogether consistent. I have as much faith, I think, as he has in human nature and in my fellow Canadians. But the minister himself says that it is the five per cent who have always spoiled it for the other ninety-five per cent, and when, just a few minutes ago, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested to the minister that we should fix the prices as from a certain date and the onus would be on those who felt justified to make an

War Exchange Conservation Act
application, the minister said that there would be so many applications that we would be swamped, that it would take a tremendous amount of administrative machinery to handle all the innumerable cases of persons who would be applying to have prices increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, legitimately in most
cases.

That is the very 'point. If there is that large number of people in Canada who will think that the situation warrants an increase in price, there is all the more reason why some machinery should be set up to deal with the matter and see whether or not that increase is justified.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is certainly not talking with his customary clearness of mind, is he? The fact that a great many applicants would make applications does not mean that they would be taking an unjust advantage of the act at all. I would anticipate thousands and perhaps tens of thousands of applications on legitimate grounds. They would all have to be checked, and there would be an extensive civil service to check these legitimate applications. Is there any inconsistency in what I said? I cannot see it.

Yes. The
minister says that there is a great deal of decency in Canada and that there are a great many people who are not going to gouge out the last dollar. That is true. But the minister also knows that there was war profiteering in days gone by. The story of the last war is filled with it. The minister knows that the cost of living has risen. The minister belongs to a party which for half a century in this country has always said that the moment you give to the country a large measure of protection, you give to a small class an opportunity to exploit the public, and that is why they have talked about freedom of trade and have been opposed to high protection. But this is high protection of the very highest sort, because it is a complete embargo on certain goods. And we ask the minister to give us some assurance that, when this is applied, the public interest will be protected and the consumer will not be exploited.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. I will give that.

Before the resolution as amended carries, I should like to say a word in commendation of the minister's department, on the ground that I believe they have exercised their powers wisely, with restraint and effectiveness. There have been
rises in prices in Canada, but no such extravagant prices as were registered in the last war.
I would say that on the whole the increases have been justified from the producers' point of view, although they have been painful to the consumers, and before very long adjustments will have to be made on behalf of the consumers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the Minister of Labour who should be congratulated.

Well, I don't know. These boards are becoming so bewildering that it is impossible for a person to keep track of them without a guide; but let the credit go to whomsoever it should go. The work has been well done.
But there is one matter which I wish to draw to the minister's attention. The other day, when we were discussing the application of the principles of social credit, we came to the question of price.
The committee will remember how almost hysterical the minister became when he envisaged all the spies in every shop and the tremendous regimentation and all that. He is now confronted with the same kind of problem, and he says, " Well, wherever there is a salesman there is going to be a buyer, and we will hear about it." I would just suggest to the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We were talking about
rationing-price-fixing and rationing.

I would just suggest to the minister that the next time he meditates such references to the principles of social credit and the just price as he made the other day-which I have not had an opportunity to answer, but which I am going to answer some of these days-he should just go back and read this fine statement he made in reply to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He will then discover that this matter of controlling price is not an insuperable problem, that when the problem is attacked with scientific skill and determination, and on certain scientific principles, it can be controlled, and without a whole lot of spies too. I thought I would just make that comment because I believe the minister needs it.
